rows.note_text: RIVER VIEW NEUROLOGY SERVICE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel Harbour View Medical Centre 12 Quayside Road, Bristol, BS1 5AB Dear Dr Patel Michael Turner, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H728391 NHS No. 9473826150 Flat 3, 28 Millpond Lane, Bristol, BS2 0DR I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today for ongoing follow-up of his seizures. I last saw him in March this year. Since then, his events have continued at a fairly regular cadence, occurring roughly once every seven to ten days. He feels that the frequency has not shifted since our previous review despite good adherence to medication. Current medicines as reported today are: Carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily, Levetiracetam 1250 mg twice daily, Topiramate 100 mg twice daily, Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily, and Clobazam 10 mg at night. He notes manageable daytime sleepiness and occasional light-headedness on standing, without clear triggers for the events. He denies rashes but mentions intermittent tingling in his calves after longer walks. There have been no injuries, hospitalisations, or episodes requiring rescue therapy. His partner has observed brief spells of reduced responsiveness on two occasions over the past month, each lasting under a minute, with rapid recovery and no confusion. He has also had one larger event about two weeks ago, witnessed at home, with whole-body stiffening and shaking described by his partner; recovery took approximately 30 minutes. These patterns are in keeping with his previous reports and remain at the same tempo. Sleep deprivation and missed meals seem to precede some attacks, though he is making efforts to maintain regular routines. Neurological examination today is unremarkable. Weight and blood pressure are stable. We discussed safety, work routines, and strategies to minimise sleep disruption. He is keen to avoid medication changes until after further diagnostic clarification. I have arranged ambulatory EEG monitoring within the next month to better characterise the events and to guide any subsequent adjustments. Until we have the recording results, I have advised him to continue his current regimen as above and to keep a simple diary noting any aura-like symptoms, potential precipitants, and recovery details. I will review him in clinic once the monitoring is completed. In the meantime, he has contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for practical advice and support. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 06 November 2020 Dr Wang Saffron Park Hospital Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL Dear Dr Wang John Doe, DOB: 09-02-1941, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746 Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today by video link with the ward team. He is a bedbound older adult residing in a nursing facility, and most of the history was provided by his named nurse and the weekday caregiver, who also maintain a seizure observation log. The caregiving staff report variability in recent events, noting “one or three seizures last month” depending on which entries were counted as full events versus brief episodes without clear impairment. They describe brief behavioural arrest with unresponsiveness, occasional right arm tremor, and post-event confusion lasting up to 20 minutes. There has been no reported tongue biting or head injury. No clear daytime pattern; some episodes occurred around early morning care. The team deny intercurrent infection, but he has had reduced oral intake on some days. He is currently on Levetiracetam 750 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 50 mg b.d., administered crushed with soft food. He has tolerated these without rash or clear mood change. The nurse notes intermittent daytime somnolence and mild dizziness on sitting up, which may be multifactorial given his frailty and concurrent medications for blood pressure and constipation. They also report occasional myoclonic jerks during repositioning, which are not clearly time-linked to the recorded seizures. Examination today was limited by the remote setting. He was rousable to voice, oriented to person, followed one-step commands inconsistently, with no focal asymmetry appreciated on gross limb movements. No cardiorespiratory distress. Skin intact with pressure-relief measures in place. Most observations were relayed by staff. Plan: - Continue current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for now given the nursing team’s report of “one or three seizures last month” and the uncertainty about which events represent definite seizures. - The facility will maintain a structured seizure diary capturing: exact time, witnessed features (including eye deviation, limb involvement, automatisms), duration, recovery phase, possible triggers (missed doses, sleep disruption, infection), and pre-event observations. - Arrange serum levels for Lamotrigine and routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC) through the nursing facility within the next two weeks to check for metabolic contributors and adherence proxies; ensure results are forwarded to the clinic. - Request an in-reach community EEG if feasible to help characterise events, acknowledging the limitations in a bedbound patient. - Nursing advice: maintain strict medication administration times, ensure hydration, and continue pressure-area care. Observe for any new focal deficits or prolonged events (>5 minutes), for which emergency protocols should be followed. - We will review in 8–10 weeks via telemedicine with the same caregivers present and the updated seizure diary to guide any medication adjustments. Please let me know if there are changes in his baseline cognition, suspected infection, or if the events escalate in frequency or duration before the planned review. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 02 August 2024 10:15 To: epilepsy.clinic@kch.nhs.uk Cc: Dr Michael O’Connor (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Emily Chen (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Review and medication adjustment Dear Dr Patel, Epilepsy diagnosis: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The patient reports events consistent with both generalised seizures and focal seizures, including brief focal aware sensory auras that sometimes progress, as well as separate episodes with generalised onset. Current medication: 1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily 2. Topiramate 50 mg twice daily Current seizure frequency: The patient reports uncertainty when recalling counts due to clustering; they believe there were 3 or 5 seizures last month. Two were typical brief focal aware episodes with right-hand paraesthesia and preserved awareness, and one to three events were generalised with loss of awareness, a brief convulsion, and post-event myalgia lasting several hours. No clear precipitant identified beyond poor sleep in the week prior. Assessment: The history supports co-existing generalised and focal seizure types. There has been an apparent increase in generalised events over the last month despite good adherence and stable lamotrigine levels (patient-reported, awaiting serum confirmation). They deny intercurrent illness or new psychoactive substances. They note heightened stress at work and occasional missed meals, which may lower seizure threshold. Plan of action: - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. - Increase topiramate to 75 mg twice daily for two weeks, then 100 mg twice daily if tolerated. Discussed potential cognitive side effects and the need for adequate hydration. - If further generalised events occur despite this, we will consider adding valproate if not contraindicated, or brivaracetam as an alternative; final choice to be guided by tolerability and comorbidities at next review. - Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) and routine EEG with sleep deprivation to better characterise both focal and generalised features. - Safety advice reinforced: no driving in accordance with DVLA guidance; avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol binges; ensure supervised bathing. - Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if further clusters occur. With best wishes,

rows.note_text: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 20 November 2021 Dr Susan University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Susan, William Harris, DOB: 15-02-1965, Hospital No: H563829 NHS No. 9273645810 10 Meadow Park, London, EC1V 9BT Summary/Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with impaired awareness; history of traumatic brain injury; travel-related anxiety; osteoporosis; former alcohol dependence (in sustained remission); hypertension; hyperlipidaemia. Currently residing in supported accommodation. Smoker. Medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily; Carbamazepine (Tegretol Retard) 400 mg twice daily; Topiramate 75 mg morning and 100 mg evening; Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily; Lansoprazole 30 mg once daily; Bisoprolol 5 mg once daily; Ramipril 5 mg once daily; Thiamine 100 mg once daily; Vitamin B compound strong one tablet daily; Calcium/Vitamin D supplements; Carbocisteine 750 mg twice daily; Emollients as required. I reviewed Bill in clinic today, accompanied by his key worker from the residence. He remains engaged with routines and reports improved appetite. He uses a single-point stick outdoors and is independent indoors. No recent falls. Sleep has improved since a change to a quieter room. He continues to abstain from alcohol and attends weekly wellbeing sessions. Focal epilepsy: Bill describes stereotyped focal impaired-awareness episodes featuring a rising epigastric sensation, brief arrest of speech, right facial pulling, and post-event confusion for several minutes. Importantly, he and staff document 5 or 7 focal onset seizures in three weeks during a recent period that included an episode while travelling by air. He links this cluster to marked anticipatory and in-flight anxiety, sleep disruption the night before travel, and missed hydration. Outside that three‑week window, there have been no further episodes for the last six weeks. There has been no secondary generalisation, tongue biting, or injuries. No clear intercurrent infection. Medication adherence is generally good; one evening dose of levetiracetam may have been late on the day of outbound travel. Travel context: Bill acknowledges travel anxiety, particularly around security checks and take-off. He is open to structured preparation and timing medication around flight schedules. No panic attacks outside travel. Examination: Afebrile, BP 132/78 mmHg, pulse 66 bpm regular. Neurological exam unchanged: mild increased tone right upper limb, subtle right pronator drift, gait slightly wide-based but safe with stick. No focal tenderness; feet intact, no callosities today. Cognition stable to brief screening; orientation preserved. Plan: - Diagnosis reaffirmed as focal epilepsy. Maintain current anti-seizure regimen without dose change, given six seizure-free weeks following the travel-related cluster. - Provide a written travel plan: ensure adherence with doses timed to flight schedule, maintain sleep the night before, regular hydration, and avoidance of excess caffeine. Airport letter supplied to carry medicines in hand luggage. - Offer brief anxiety management strategies and signpost to primary care for short-term psychological support focused on travel anxiety. - Safety advice reinforced: no swimming unsupervised, avoid heights, and comply with DVLA guidance—he is not driving. - Bloods: request U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, and carbamazepine level via practice in the next two weeks. - Bone health: continue calcium/vitamin D; DEXA recheck due next year. - Follow-up: neurology clinic in 6 months, sooner if further clusters or any generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Yours sincerely,

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 05 April 2023 Dr A. Patel Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr A. Patel Consultant Neurologist, Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1982, Hospital No: KCH742915 NHS No. 9065183274 78 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 2LP Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He attended with his partner and provided a clear diary of recent events. Unfortunately, there is evidence of clinical deterioration over the past month. He reports increased day-to-day difficulty with concentration, intermittent word-finding pauses, and escalating fatigue and irritability that he attributes to his current polytherapy. Adverse effects are becoming bothersome (notably daytime somnolence, unsteadiness on rapid head turns, and blunted mood), yet seizure control remains suboptimal. Over the last week he recorded five focal cognitive and six focal non-motors in last week, occurring at variable times without an obvious precipitant. Several of these were clustered over two consecutive mornings, with prolonged post-event disorientation on one occasion. His partner also notes brief nocturnal arousals with confusion, though no clear witnessed generalised convulsions. He remains adherent to medication and has not missed doses; he denies alcohol or illicit substance use. Sleep has been fragmented, in part due to early-morning awakenings. He is using a smartphone seizure diary, and we reviewed consistent timestamped entries. There has been no recent intercurrent illness. He has not driven and understands the DVLA guidance as previously discussed. Examination today was non-focal. Gait was steady on slow turns but he felt light-headed on tandem stepping. No papilloedema. Cardiovascular and systemic review unremarkable. Mood was subdued but there was no thought disorder or psychotic features. Investigations to date include a prior routine EEG (last year) that was non-diagnostic and a brain MRI (18 months ago) reported as structurally unremarkable. Given the current pattern and the worsening frequency and impact, I am concerned that, despite polytherapy, control is not adequate and tolerability is poor. We discussed the need to clarify the electroclinical pattern and to consider rationalisation of treatment if safe to do so. He is agreeable to expedited prolonged video-EEG monitoring as an inpatient, and I will request this urgently. I will also arrange updated bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D, thyroid function) and drug levels where available to check for toxicity or interactions contributing to the adverse effects. We reviewed general measures: regular sleep schedule, hydration, and avoidance of missed meals. He and his partner are aware of seizure first aid and have a plan to escalate if events become longer or different in character. I provided contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for interim support while we await telemetry. I will update you once monitoring is completed and results are available. In the meantime, I have not altered his current regimen today due to the risk of further destabilisation, but the trajectory is concerning, and I anticipate we may need to rationalise therapy soon depending on monitoring findings and tolerability. Yours sincerely

Patel Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr A. Patel Consultant Neurologist, Daniel Roberts, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K742918 NHS No. 9065173342 12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 8TR Thank you for asking me to review your patient. We discussed his known generalised epilepsy and recent symptom pattern. He described a clear increase in events over the last quarter, noting two drop attacks and nine convulsions in the past three months. His partner corroborates these figures from a seizure diary kept on her phone. There is no consistent diurnal pattern; most convulsions have occurred from wakefulness, with two events out of sleep. Recovery has been uncomplicated, with post‑ictal confusion lasting 15–30 minutes and no focal neurological deficits afterwards. He denies new head injury, alcohol escalation, or intercurrent illness. He reports past variability in pharmacy supply, with occasional brand and formulation switches documented in his records; historically this has impacted adherence at times. He states he has made a concerted effort over the last month to maintain regular dosing and has arranged repeat prescriptions earlier to avoid gaps. rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Kate Health Centre Keele University, Keele, Newcastle Staffordshire ST5 5BG Dear Dr Kate Elliot Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: K593012 NHS No. 7712048891 12 Willow Bank, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 3PA Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with predominantly nocturnal events as per partner reports; partner was not present at today’s review. No family history of epilepsy volunteered. Current seizure pattern and history: The patient describes disrupted sleep and unrefreshing mornings, with tongue soreness on two occasions and bedclothes disarray. Although the partner was not present today, prior collateral history has suggested night-time events. Over the past two months, the patient reports three focal onset seizures and three focal automatisms in the past two months, occurring in the context of otherwise predominantly nocturnal generalised events. Daytime awareness lapses have been brief without injury. No reported status epilepticus. No clear catamenial pattern. Alcohol intake minimal; no recreational drugs. Medication history: Currently on Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily (started 2020, partial response, weight gain), and Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily (added 2022, mood irritability but acceptable). Rescue: Buccal midazolam held at home—unused in the past year. Previously tried and stopped due to side effects or inefficacy: Lamotrigine (rash), Topiramate (cognitive slowing, paresthesia), Zonisamide (poor appetite), Clobazam (sedation). No known medication allergies. Relevant comorbidities: Mild asthma (inhaled beclometasone as needed). Migraine without aura approximately monthly. No known cardiac disease. Last vitamin D low–normal (2024). Driving: not driving and aware of DVLA guidance. Interim history since last review: Sleep schedule irregular due to shift work. Stress at work reported. No recent infections. Reports adherence to medication with occasional late evening doses. Has begun keeping a diary; smartwatch data suggests nocturnal movement clusters twice weekly. Examination today: Well-appearing, oriented, normal speech, no focal neurological deficits. Weight stable over the past year. Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular. Investigations: Repeat serum valproate level to be checked (trough). U&E, LFTs, FBC requested. Consider repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to capture generalised discharges and nocturnal events; ambulatory EEG if scheduling delays. Plan: - Generalised epilepsy: Given ongoing nocturnal events and the pattern over the past two months (three focal onset seizures and three focal automatisms in the past two months alongside suspected generalised events), we will prioritise sleep optimisation and adherence. If levels therapeutic yet events persist, discuss swap from Levetiracetam to Brivaracetam for mood tolerability, or consideration of Perampanel as adjunct, balancing side-effect profile. The patient understands this staged approach. - Safety: Night-time precautions discussed (low bed height, remove sharp furniture edges, partner to use side positioning if safe, consider bed alarm). Buccal midazolam supply to be checked in date. Seizure diary to continue. - Lifestyle: Advice on regular sleep routine despite shifts; sleep hygiene leaflet provided. Limit alcohol. Encourage vitamin D supplementation and weight maintenance. - DVLA: Patient is not driving and will continue to follow DVLA regulations for epilepsy. - Follow-up: Nurse telephone check-in in 6 weeks to review seizure diary, sleep schedule, and blood results. Clinic review in 4 months, earlier if events escalate or injuries occur. Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are concerns or if workplace adjustments for stable shifts are feasible. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 08 October 2019 Dr Patel Riverside Health Centre 1 Wharf Lane, Southwark, London SE1 2AB Dear Dr Patel Wendy Brown, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: K482715 NHS No. 6592841037 Flat 7 Brookside Avenue, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 2QD Diagnoses/summary: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Occupational context: Works in a cold-chain warehouse (sustained low temperatures). Gloves and chilled environment can slow fine-motor handling of rescue devices, especially during post-ictal periods. Current presentation: I reviewed Wendy Brown in clinic today; she attended alone. She describes ongoing focal aware and focal impaired-awareness episodes with auras of rising epigastric discomfort and transient speech arrest, sometimes with lip smacking. She has had occasional tonic-clonic over last year, typically evolving from focal onset and tending to cluster during periods of sleep deprivation or shift changes at work. She carries a rescue benzodiazepine; however, she reports that in sub-zero bays the zip on the pouch can stick and gloves slow administration, leading to delay of a few minutes. She is exploring a pouch with a larger pull tab and a front-zip uniform pocket. She has no history of glaucoma; vision checks up to date. Mood stable; no recent depression or psychosis. She requested a concise seizure action plan card; we provided this today, including when to call 999. - Sleep and shifts: Advised consistent sleep windows where rota permits; she will request fewer rapid turnarounds between night and early shifts. She will track seizures relative to shift pattern in a diary. - Follow-up: Routine review in 3 months, sooner if increased seizure frequency, adverse effects, or any visual symptoms (â€ warning given regarding acute eye pain/redness). rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Anil Rao Riverside Health Centre 12 Meadowbank, Southwark London SE1 9XX Dear Dr Anil Rao Sophie Turner, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: H739264 NHS No. 8826405172 Flat 3, 29 Mill Wharf, Deptford, London SE8 3JL Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures with deteriorating control; prior routine and ambulatory EEGs reported non-diagnostic. MRI brain (2017) structurally unremarkable. No established provoking metabolic cause. Co-morbid migraine without aura, intermittent. Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural adverse effects, minimal efficacy), Carbamazepine (dizziness, hyponatraemia), Sodium valproate (weight gain; discontinued), Lamotrigine (partial benefit previously), Clobazam PRN (sedation), Lacosamide (ataxia), Topiramate (cognitive slowing), Zonisamide (insomnia). Not taken: Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Rufinamide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine. I reviewed Sophie Turner in clinic today. She attended alone and provided a detailed history corroborated by diary entries and two workplace incident reports. She describes a clear deterioration over the past fortnight with events evolving faster than previously, now predominantly occurring in bright, high-noise environments such as stage rigging areas and a metal fabrication bay on the factory floor. She notes that premonitory sensations, when present, are shorter (seconds rather than minutes), and colleagues have observed earlier onset of impaired awareness and automatisms compared with her prior pattern. She has also noted increased post-event fatigue and headaches. Seizure frequency and pattern: Prior to this recent deterioration, this month so far she has 2 seizures; earlier two in Aug, 0 in Jul and one in Jun, over waking hours and sleep. In contrast, over the last fortnight she has had seven to nine seizures during the last two weeks, with two requiring supervision at work. No clear alcohol, sleep deprivation, or intercurrent illness triggers were identified beyond the bright, high-noise settings. No tongue biting or urinary incontinence has been reported in the recent cluster; recoveries have been slower. Medications at review: - Lamotrigine 100 mg morning, 150 mg evening (self-reported adherence; last level pending) - Clobazam 10 mg at night, additional 5–10 mg PRN for clusters (used twice in the last week) - Folic acid 5 mg daily Adverse effects reported: daytime somnolence with PRN clobazam; otherwise tolerating current baseline regimen. Mood stable. No visual blurring or diplopia. Weight stable. No new neurological deficits between events. Examination today: Alert and oriented, speech fluent, cranial nerves intact, no lateralising motor signs, gait normal. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. No photoparoxysmal response provoked with simple office-based light challenge, though this is not a substitute for formal testing. Investigations: Last MRI brain (2017) normal. Prior routine EEGs non-specific; sleep-deprived EEG (2019) without epileptiform discharges. Bloods (April 2025) normal including sodium and LFTs. New bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D) and lamotrigine level sent today; results to be copied to you. Risk and functional impact: The escalation in frequency and acceleration of event evolution, particularly in high-stimulus workplaces, represents a clear deterioration in control with increased risk of injury. She has self-restricted tasks at height and is temporarily avoiding strobe-lit stages. She no longer drives. Plan: - Safety: Advised strict adherence to workplace modifications already initiated by occupational health; avoid work at height and unsupervised tasks near moving machinery until stability improves. Seizure first aid refreshed; written advice provided for employer. - Monitoring: Provided a structured seizure diary template and asked her to record environmental exposures (light/noise levels) and sleep. Offered video capture where safe and feasible. - Investigations: Urgent outpatient prolonged video-EEG monitoring request submitted, with photic stimulation and sound sensitivity protocols, to characterise current events given the recent deterioration. Repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol requested in view of change in semiology. - Medications: No abrupt changes today given recent clustering. Will review lamotrigine level; if subtherapeutic, consider cautious dose optimisation. Should further clusters occur, advised PRN clobazam may be used as already prescribed, within agreed limits; she understands sedation risk. Alternative options discussed for future consideration (patient-informed): brivaracetam or perampanel, acknowledging prior behavioural effects with levetiracetam. - Support: Epilepsy specialist nurse to telephone within 1–2 weeks to reassess frequency and review safety measures. Provided information on trigger management in high-stimulus environments and reasonable workplace adjustments. - Follow-up: Rapid-access review in 6 weeks or sooner if events escalate, loss of consciousness with injury, or new neurological symptoms. Given the recent increase to seven to nine seizures during the last two weeks, I am concerned about ongoing instability and have flagged her investigations as urgent. I will update you when results are available and will coordinate medication adjustments accordingly. Thank you for your continued care. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Priya Anand Holloway Road Health Centre 192 Holloway Road London N7 8DL Dear Dr Priya Anand Jordan Patel, DOB: 14-03-1990, Hospital No: H937214 NHS No. 7843206159 Flat 12, 6 Arterton Close, London N1 0PH Diagnoses/summary: Focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Ongoing events with convulsion weekly despite current regimen and dietary therapy. No known structural lesion on prior imaging per historical reports. Ketogenic/modified diet: Patient is following a supervised modified ketogenic diet (external provider). Recorded plan: 3:1 fat-to-combined protein/carbohydrate ratio; carbohydrate limited to approximately 20–25 g/day; fluid intake target 2.0–2.5 L/day; medium-chain triglyceride oil 15 mL with breakfast and evening meal; vitamin/mineral supplementation as per diet protocol (multivitamin, selenium 55 mcg/day, vitamin D3 1000 IU/day). Diet initiated March 2025; monitored by dietetics team elsewhere with monthly telehealth reviews. Patient reports improved alertness in the morning and reduced post-event fatigue, but seizure frequency remains at convulsion weekly. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily - Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily - Folic acid 5 mg once daily - Omeprazole 20 mg once daily (dyspepsia) Previous medication trials (ineffective or poorly tolerated): Carbamazepine (dizziness), valproate (weight gain, mood), lacosamide (somnolence), clobazam PRN (sedation), gabapentin (no benefit). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, perampanel, or pregabalin. Allergies: No known drug allergies. History since last review: I saw the patient today unaccompanied. They report adherence to both medicines and diet with a written log. Typical focal onset features include epigastric rising sensation, brief speech arrest, and right facial automatisms, evolving on occasion to bilateral tonic–clonic activity. The overall pattern over the past two months has been stable at convulsion weekly, usually in the late evening, with post-ictal confusion lasting 30–45 minutes. There have been no injuries, tongue biting once in August, and no prolonged events requiring rescue therapy. No clear dietary triggers identified; sleep curtailment and high work stress appear to lower threshold per patient account. They continue to drive abstinent in line with DVLA regulations (self-reported). Mood is described as “variable but manageable”; no suicidal ideation; screening scores with the diet team reportedly low. Weight has fallen by 3.2 kg since commencing the modified ketogenic plan; hydration is reportedly adequate. Examination: BP 118/72, pulse 72 regular, weight 68.5 kg (down from 71.7 kg in March). Neurological examination non-focal. No cutaneous stigmata. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Investigations: Historical MRI (report from 2016) described as non-lesional. Prior EEGs have shown left temporal interictal discharges per patient report; we do not yet have the raw data or formal reports from the external centre. Routine bloods requested today (U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, lipid profile, bicarbonate) to monitor dietary effects and antiepileptic drug safety. Assessment: Focal epilepsy with likely temporal lobe onset events continuing at convulsion weekly despite dual therapy and a supervised modified ketogenic diet. Some symptomatic gains reported (energy, shorter recovery) but no clear reduction in convulsive frequency. No red flags elicited today. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine and levetiracetam at current doses for now; confirm trough levels are not required by current protocol. - Obtain formal copies of prior MRI and EEG reports; consider repeat video-EEG telemetry if events remain unchanged over the next 4–6 months. - Liaise (with patient consent) with the external ketogenic/modified diet team to share outcomes data and blood results; keep current macronutrient targets unchanged pending labs. - Safety: reinforced seizure first aid and SUDEP risk discussion; patient to avoid swimming alone and heights; continue to follow DVLA guidance. - Lifestyle: maintain regular sleep schedule; patient will keep a detailed seizure and diet diary noting sleep, stress, and timing relative to meals. - Follow-up: nurse-led telephone review in 6 weeks to check events, tolerance, and lab results; clinic review in 4 months or sooner if convulsions cluster, injuries occur, or prolonged events develop. Thank you for your ongoing care and for forwarding any interim concerns. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 25 October 2018 Dr Priya Menon Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Priya Menon Consultant Neurologist, Sarah Bennett, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH728450 NHS No. 9475203681 22 Brookside Close, London, SE15 8HT Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in clinic today, accompanied by her partner and an assistance dog in training provided through a charitable programme. She reports that her habitual events have persisted over the last year and she has begun logging them with a menstrual tracking app to better understand timing. She notes that the attacks cluster around her period, with the window of vulnerability beginning a few days prior to bleeding and extending into the early days thereafter. Outside that peri-period interval, she seldom experiences events. She describes this pattern as “most episodes falling from roughly three days before the period up to three days afterwards,” which her partner’s observations broadly corroborate. The typical spell begins without warning, with a brief pause in activity and a blank facial expression. This is followed by loss of responsiveness and stiffening of both arms with a low vocal sound; on some occasions there is bilateral shaking lasting under two minutes. She is usually tired and mildly confused for 30–60 minutes afterwards, sometimes with headache. She denies clear nocturnal events, tongue biting or urinary incontinence, and has no consistent focal neurological symptoms pre- or post-event. She reports no recent head injury, febrile seizures in childhood, or family history of similar episodes. Sleep deprivation and marked stress may lower her threshold, but alcohol does not appear to be a trigger. She is not currently driving. Medication history: she is taking lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily without reported rash, and folic acid 5 mg daily. She has previously tried levetiracetam for six months but discontinued due to irritability. No known drug allergies. She uses a period-tracking diary and has begun aligning her logs with her partner’s notes and smartwatch detections of elevated heart rate during events; these data suggest the cyclical clustering described above. Examination in clinic today was unremarkable with normal cranial nerves, tone, power, coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. There were no signs of depression on brief screen, though she describes intermittent anxiety around the time of anticipated episodes. The assistance dog in training remained calm and did not interfere with the assessment; she reports the dog has been conditioned to alert her partner when she becomes unresponsive, which has improved safety at home. Prior investigations: routine EEG six months ago was within normal limits. MRI brain (1.5T) last year was reported as structurally normal. Bloods including U&E, LFT, glucose, thyroid function and prolactin (post-event sampling not obtained) have been unremarkable. Cycle tracking notes were shown on her phone and suggest the temporal clustering stated above. Impression: ongoing recurrent events with a clear temporal association to the menstrual cycle as described. At present I cannot provide a single unifying classification of the events from the information available. The pattern and witness accounts warrant further characterisation. Plan: - I have requested ambulatory EEG with event button capture timed across the late luteal to early follicular phase next cycle, as she reliably experiences events within that interval. - Repeat high-resolution MRI brain (3T) with epilepsy protocol to be arranged. - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily for now; she prefers to avoid changes until after the monitoring period. She understands the importance of strict adherence and will continue to log events. - Safety advice reinforced: avoid baths unsupervised, consider showering with door unlocked, caution with heights and open water, and continue partner supervision during higher-risk days as per her log. The assistance dog training team will be informed (with her consent) of monitoring dates so they can support exposure in a controlled manner. - I have provided a seizure first aid leaflet and discussed SUDEP risk in simple terms; she is aware of the benefit of regular sleep and stress management. - We discussed that if the cyclical pattern is consistently demonstrated on monitoring, we could explore time-targeted strategies in liaison with her GP and gynaecology colleagues. I will review her in clinic after the ambulatory EEG and MRI are completed. Please let me know if I can provide any further information. Thank you again for involving me in her care. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel Maple Gate Health Centre 12 Brook Street, London W1D 3QF Dear Dr Patel, Aisha Khan, DOB: 04-11-1992, Hospital No: H847520 NHS No. 9054317762 Flat 3, 29 Crescent Court, London, NW1 8AL Medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Patient reports good tolerability with occasional fatigue. Uses buccal midazolam 10 mg as rescue, not required in the past seven months. I reviewed the multiple recent ED triage records and nursing documentation. These relate to brief attendances earlier this year for possible auras and one episode of anxiety with palpitations; no generalised convulsive activity was documented, observations were stable, and she was discharged after reassurance and advice. Since her last clinic review and after consolidating her dosing routine with a pill organiser, she describes her seizure control as Better over the past seven months. She has not required rescue medication in that period and there have been no injuries or admissions. She continues to notice occasional sleep disruption linked to shift work; she is trialling a fixed bedtime schedule and avoiding missed doses, which she feels has helped. Neurological examination in clinic today was unremarkable. There are no new focal symptoms, and she denies adverse neuropsychiatric effects beyond mild fatigue. She keeps a seizure diary and brings ED leaflets from prior visits; the timelines align with improved control since March. We discussed common triggers, the importance of adherence, and safety advice including driving regulations and first‑aid guidance; she confirms she is not currently driving and will update the DVLA only in accordance with legal criteria if appropriate in future. Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily unchanged. - Maintain seizure diary and sleep hygiene measures; avoid missed doses. - Rescue buccal midazolam to remain available; no changes required. - If breakthrough events recur, we will consider serum levels and alternative add‑on therapy; she will contact us sooner via the epilepsy nurse line if this occurs. - Routine follow‑up in six months, sooner if problems. Yours sincerely

Present Medication: 1. Carbamazepine (Tegretol Retard) 600 mg twice daily 2. Levetiracetam (Keppra) 500 mg twice daily Present Seizure Frequency: Over the past week on the hot line in a high‑heat, fast‑paced commercial kitchen, the patient documented sz X2/d, typically clustering near the end of the dinner rush when ambient grill temperatures and dehydration were most pronounced. Colleagues described brief right‑hand automatisms and staring (focal) on some days, and on two occasions this escalated to generalised tonic‑clonic activity with rapid recovery after being guided to a cooler prep area. History and Context: The patient works as a line cook on sautÃ‚Â·Ã©/grill, frequently exposed to 40+Â°C ambient heat, flashing oil, and continuous ticket pressure. They report prodromal tingling in the left face with a metallic taste (suggestive of focal onset) during peak service, occasionally followed by a sudden generalised convulsion without clear warning. There is no recent illness, sleep deprivation beyond standard split shifts, or missed medication; hydration may be suboptimal despite attempts to rotate to the walk‑in. Kitchen CCTV and supervisor incident logs corroborate the timing (between 19:30–21:00). No head injury reported; no alcohol on shift; no use of recreational substances. rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr A. Malik Riverside Health Centre 12 Stonebridge Way Southwark London SE1 5JT Dear Dr A. Malik Jordan Ellis, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 8439201756 Flat 3, 28 Wharf Street, London SE8 4DN Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent unprovoked seizures with ongoing events; prior routine EEG reported as non-diagnostic; brain MRI (2023) structurally normal; ongoing occupational risk due to warehouse duties between tall racking and narrow aisles Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (rash after titration), Carbamazepine (dizziness), Sodium valproate (weight gain, tremor), Lacosamide (no clear benefit), Clobazam PRN (sedation) Not taken: Topiramate, Zonisamide, Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Rufinamide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine Occupational context: Works as a warehouse picker in narrow aisles between tall racking; shift patterns vary with differing lifting demands and pace. Reports that rushing during late shifts increases stress and poor sleep. Has used a voice-activated headset for picking which is sometimes disorientating during post-event confusion. I reviewed Jordan Ellis in clinic today. They attended alone. They report ongoing brief losses of awareness with sudden behavioural arrest and occasional falls. Frequency currently described as "sz x3/d" on their seizure diary, with clustering on late shifts. They note pre-event sensations of light-headedness, ringing in the ears, and a rising nausea on some days, but at other times events occur without warning. Post-event fatigue lasts 20–40 minutes. No tongue-biting or urinary incontinence reported recently. A witness at work described staring, dropping the handheld scanner, and a slow return to baseline. No clear alcohol excess; caffeine 2–3 cups/day. Sleep fragmented on rotating shifts. Investigations: Routine EEG (2024) non-diagnostic; no interictal epileptiform activity captured. MRI brain (2023) reported no focal cortical abnormalities. Bloods (Aug 2025): FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT within reference range; vitamin D low–normal. No known head injury. No family history of epilepsy reported. Current medication: - Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily (initiated by prior team; modest reduction in duration but not frequency) - Folic acid 5 mg daily (precautionary) - Omeprazole 20 mg daily (dyspepsia) Adverse effects: Reports occasional low mood and reduced motivation since starting brivaracetam; denies suicidality. No visual symptoms or rash. Functional/safety considerations: Given the warehouse role between tall racking and narrow aisles, we discussed immediate safety measures: stepping away from elevated pallets when feeling unwell, informing a supervisor of ongoing events, and avoiding climbing or working at height. They do not operate forklifts. Has a personal alarm badge but not consistently used. Plan: - Continue brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily for now. I have provided written information and discussed potential titration options at follow-up depending on tolerability and effect. - Arrange ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) aiming to capture typical events, timed across two shift patterns if possible. - Repeat bloods including vitamin D and brivaracetam level (baseline) before any dose change. - Seizure diary to continue; patient to record shift type, sleep duration, and any missed meals alongside event times to correlate with "sz x3/d" entries. - Occupational advice letter (separate) to employer recommending avoidance of tasks at height and working alone in narrow aisles until better control is achieved; encourage buddy system during late shifts. - Lifestyle measures discussed: sleep regularity where feasible, hydration, and pacing during high-demand shifts; patient to trial pre-shift snack to mitigate light-headedness. - DVLA guidance reiterated; patient confirms they are not driving. - Follow-up in 8–10 weeks, sooner if deterioration or adverse effects. If ambulatory EEG captures typical events, we will review therapeutic options including alternative agents not yet tried. Thank you for your ongoing care and prescription support. Please let me know if you or the patient have any concerns before the next appointment. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Ayesha Rahman Southside Health Centre 12 Brook Lane, London SE15 3QT Dear Dr Ayesha Rahman Amelia Carter, DOB: 14-03-1996, Hospital No: H928417 NHS No. 8035619240 Flat 3, 29 Alder Grove, London SE23 2LP Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with catamenial pattern suspected; patient-reported clustering around menses. Clinical Summary and Context: The patient reports an intense workload with extended hours and compressed deadlines. Events tend to cluster on workdays per patient report, particularly after consecutive late finishes. There is no clear intercurrent illness, sleep has been reduced to 5–6 hours, and caffeine intake has increased. No missed doses admitted, though one delayed evening dose last week. No new head injury, alcohol or recreational drug use reported. Plan of Action: - Urgent optimisation: Increase levetiracetam from 750 mg to 1,000 mg twice daily for one week, then to 1,250 mg twice daily if tolerated. Maintain lamotrigine at 150 mg twice daily for now; levels to be checked in two weeks alongside U&E, LFTs, FBC. - Rescue medication: Prescribe buccal midazolam 10 mg for convulsions lasting >5 minutes or repeated convulsions without recovery; partner to be instructed on use. - Safety: Advise immediate cessation of driving and high-risk activities (heights, open water, operating machinery). Provide written seizure first-aid guidance. - Triggers and lifestyle: Patient-reported workload appears contributory. Recommend temporary workload adjustments and structured sleep schedule; provide fit note for employer for four weeks to facilitate reduced hours and recovery days after events. - Diagnostics: Arrange urgent ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) and repeat MRI brain epilepsy protocol; review prior imaging and EEG. Seizure diary to document timing, potential triggers, and any aura. - Follow-up: Rapid access review in three weeks or sooner if further convulsions occur. If events persist despite the above, we will discuss admission for video-EEG monitoring and consider alternative antiseizure medication. He does not recall most of the episode. There have been rare events during sleep where she has noticed similar rocking and a short cry, with him being difficult to rouse afterwards. Seizures: Over the past three months, the patient describes spells of increased seizure activity occurring in several stretches across the month, particularly following work travel. She reports brief focal aware episodes with lip-smacking and word-finding pauses, sometimes progressing to focal impaired awareness events lasting 1–2 minutes. There have been two instances with secondary generalisation in the last six weeks. No consistent nocturnal pattern noted. History since last review: I conducted a video consultation with Laura Bennett today. She reports that her overall control has worsened. She attributes a clear deterioration to frequent travel, during which she occasionally misses doses despite using phone reminders. She notes that days with disrupted flight schedules or late arrivals are followed by short runs of events over several days, interspersed with quieter intervals. There is no new head injury, infection, or alcohol excess. Sleep disruption is common around travel days. She has not driven since the generalised seizure in August. Examination (remote): Alert, oriented, fluent speech between events. No focal neurological deficits observed via video. Plan: - I emphasised the importance of strict adherence, particularly around travel days, and discussed practical measures (e.g., setting multiple timed alarms and carrying a pre-packed pill organiser in hand luggage). - I have requested serum lamotrigine and levetiracetam levels to be repeated in two weeks, timed as a trough, alongside U&E/LFTs. - We discussed seizure safety, SUDEP risk, and avoidance of sleep deprivation. She will continue to abstain from driving and will inform the DVLA as required. - I will review her in four weeks via telephone, sooner if further generalised seizures occur. Summary: This is a deterioration in seizure control in a patient with focal epilepsy, likely exacerbated by missed doses associated with frequent travel and sleep disruption. There is a pattern of increased activity over several portions of the month following travel, with two recent secondary generalised seizures. Yours sincerely

He reports that seizure activity has continued at intervals despite treatment adjustments, with patterns corroborated by the employer’s periodic reports. Epilepsy classification: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. He describes two clearly distinct event types. The first are generalised convulsive seizures beginning without warning, with sudden loss of awareness, bilateral tonic–clonic movements, tongue biting on occasion, and post‑ictal fatigue lasting several hours. The second are focal impaired‑awareness episodes with an initial rising epigastric sensation and auditory distortion, followed by brief behavioural arrest and right hand automatisms; he is usually confused for 5–10 minutes afterwards. He has not identified consistent triggers, though he and his line manager note that sleep restriction around shift transitions may precede both forms. Family history is negative; there is no history of significant head injury. Current frequency and recent course: By his account, events have been occurring intermittently over the past three months, with two generalised convulsions in that period and approximately four focal impaired‑awareness episodes, often clustering after a week of late shifts. Occupational health summaries dated May and August indicate similar patterns, including one witnessed generalised event on site (prompted emergency attendance, no injury). In short, the condition remains active, though day‑to‑day function between spells is preserved. Treatment: He is currently taking Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily and Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, with good adherence documented on pharmacy records and by pill counts. He reports mild irritability with Levetiracetam; otherwise tolerability is acceptable. No missed doses were admitted, though he noted two late evening doses during a recent rotation. Investigations: Prior MRI brain (2023) was structurally unremarkable. Routine EEG (2024) showed generalised spike‑and‑wave discharges and occasional left temporal sharp waves, consistent with the combined generalised and focal epilepsy phenotype described above. No new investigations since last review. Functional impact and safeguarding: He does not drive and understands DVLA guidance. Employer adjustments include avoiding lone working after night shifts for 24 hours and allocating tasks away from ladders or open water. There have been no injuries at work. He is using a seizure diary app, which aligns with the employer’s incident logs. Plan discussed today: We reviewed lifestyle measures including sleep regularity and hydration. We also discussed the option of ambulatory EEG if event patterns change, and that we will consider dose optimisation at next review if the pattern escalates. He is agreeable to continuing the current regimen for now and to share ongoing occupational health updates with the clinic. Follow‑up: I have arranged a review in four months or sooner if there is an increase in frequency, any injury, or emergence of new features (e.g., prolonged focal deficits or status). He will continue to liaise with occupational health, who will provide interim summaries. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require further information. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Amelia Carter Riverside Medical Practice 14 Brook Lane, London SE10 8JP Dear Dr Amelia Carter, Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-07-1993, Hospital No: U918274 NHS No. 4738201596 Flat 5, 21 Clarence Road, London, E5 8HB Summary/ Diagnoses: Generalised epilepsy following adolescence-onset; migraine without aura; vitamin D insufficiency corrected; former smoker, now abstinent. Lives independently and uses a seizure diary app linked to the epilepsy nurse service. Medication: - Sodium valproate modified release 500 mg twice daily. - Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily (titrated from May 2025). - Cholecalciferol 1,000 IU once daily. - Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine (maximum 2 in 24 hours). I reviewed Alex in clinic today. He attended alone and consented to sharing details from his seizure diary application, which syncs with the epilepsy nurse portal. He reports good general health, regular sleep, and no recent intercurrent illness. He has resumed light jogging three times weekly and drinks coffee occasionally, avoiding energy drinks. He has not driven and remains aware of DVLA regulations. Seizures: The diary shows infrequent events predominantly aligned with days of delayed or missed antiseizure medication (ASM) doses. Specifically: - 2025: January 0; February 1 generalised convulsion after missing evening valproate; March 0; April 0; May 1 absence cluster (3 brief events over 24 hours) after late morning lamotrigine; June 0; July 0; August 1 generalised convulsion following two consecutive late doses during a weekend trip; September 0. No injuries recorded. Postictal tiredness lasted up to 12 hours after the generalised seizures. Alex has engaged app reminders and reports improved punctuality with medications over the past six weeks. Overall pattern suggests seizures occurring in the context of irregular ASM intake rather than spontaneous breakthrough. Epilepsy classification: He has generalised epilepsy with a history of generalised tonic–clonic seizures and brief absence episodes, consistent with prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike–wave activity. No focal features reported. Examination: Alert and oriented. Speech and language normal. Cranial nerves intact. No tremor or ataxia. Gait normal. Weight stable at 76 kg (BMI 24). Investigations: - Lamotrigine trough level (July 2025) 3.4 mg/L (within target for combination therapy). - Valproate total level (July 2025) 68 mg/L. - LFTs and FBC (July 2025) within reference limits. Vitamin D now 34 ng/mL. Plan: - Continue sodium valproate MR 500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily without dose change. - Reinforce adherence strategies: app-based alarms retained; pharmacy blister pack to start next month as arranged. - Safety: continue to avoid driving; maintain supervision for swimming and avoid heights; first-aid guidance reviewed. - Migraine: continue sumatriptan as needed; no interaction issues noted at current doses. - Bloods: repeat LFTs, FBC, and drug levels in December 2025 or sooner if clinical change. - Follow-up in 6 months with interim review by epilepsy nurse if further logged events occur. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Citygate Neurology Clinic Department of Clinical Neurosciences Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Emily Carter Citygate Health Centre 12 Albion Street, Manchester M1 4AB Dear Dr Emily Carter, William Harris, DOB: 15-02-1965, Hospital No: H563829 NHS No. 9273645810 10 Meadow Park, London, EC1V 9BT Summary/Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with sensory-motor onset, previous traumatic brain injury, progressive cognitive slowing and executive dysfunction, osteoporosis, past alcohol dependence (currently abstinent), lives in supported accommodation, active smoker. Medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily; Carbamazepine MR 400 mg twice daily; Topiramate 75 mg morning and 100 mg evening; Thiamine; Calcium/Vitamin D; Atorvastatin; Lansoprazole; Bisoprolol; Ramipril; Carbocisteine; Emollients. I reviewed Bill in clinic today, accompanied by his key worker who has supported him for the last year. He reports increasing sensory intolerance to brightly lit, acoustically harsh environments. Over the last six months he describes more rapid-onset events with left facial pulling followed by jerking of the left arm, preserved awareness, then brief speech arrest. These episodes now arise chiefly during shifts near stage lighting rigs at his day centre and on the factory floor during machinery testing, with faster evolution than previously described. Seizures: He remains abstinent from alcohol; however, he and staff note a pattern of attacks clustering after evenings spent in loud, high-glare venues at the centre, consistent with episodes that tend to follow exposure rather than intake. Frequency has increased: July x 3 focal aware motor; August x 4 focal aware motor (two progressing to impaired awareness); September x 5 focal aware motor with two focal to bilateral tonic–clonic. This represents a clear deterioration compared with earlier months when events were sporadic and slower in onset. A seizure diary kept by staff corroborates this trend, particularly on days involving rigging under bright LED arrays and during compressor testing. Neurological examination: Alert and oriented; speech mildly hesitant. Subtle left nasolabial flattening at rest. Increased tone right lower limb with circumduction on gait testing; Romberg negative. No new cranial nerve deficits. Fundoscopy unremarkable. Cognitive screen shows slowed processing speed compared with prior review. Epilepsy classification: The clinical semiology, consistent lateralising signs, and evolution support a diagnosis of focal epilepsy. There is no evidence of a primary generalised epilepsy syndrome. Risk/precipitating factors: Photopic glare and complex acoustic environments appear to act as triggers. Sleep is fragmented on nights after late activities at the centre. No current alcohol use. Plan: - Acknowledge deterioration with increased event rate and faster evolution in bright, high-noise settings. - Arrange urgent EEG with photic stimulation and patterned stimulus, plus prolonged ambulatory recording across a typical day at the centre if feasible. - MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to reassess focal cortical injury sequelae post-TBI. - No immediate change to antiepileptic regimen today pending investigations; consider levetiracetam uptitration versus switch to lacosamide at next review, guided by EEG and tolerability. - Provide written guidance to day centre to minimise triggers: reduce exposure to intense LED arrays, allow shaded rest areas, use hearing protection during machinery testing, scheduled breaks to reduce sensory load. - Reinforce seizure diary with precise logging of lighting/sound exposure and sleep the preceding night. - Check trough carbamazepine level, U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D. - Bone health: continue Calcium/Vitamin D; DEXA due next year. Follow-up: Review in 8 weeks, sooner if further focal to bilateral tonic–clonic events occur. Yours sincerely,

She reports clusters of brief nocturnal warning sensations followed by loss of awareness on three occasions in September and two further events in early October. This worsening appears to coincide with a change to regular night shifts and curtailed sleep, and she feels that disrupted sleep patterns reliably precede the events by 24–48 hours. She also notes increased fatigue and difficulty recovering after each episode. Her partner witnessed the most recent event and described a blank stare, unresponsiveness for approximately one minute, and subsequent confusion lasting 10–15 minutes without tongue biting or incontinence. There have been no injuries. She has not been driving. Headaches have been more frequent after nights on duty, and she has been taking simple analgesics no more than three times per week. She denies alcohol excess or recreational drug use. Menses are regular and she has not noticed a cyclical pattern. On review today, neurological examination is unremarkable. Routine bloods from last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs) were within reference ranges. She has not previously had prolonged sleep deprivation provocation in EEG, and her last EEG two years ago was non-diagnostic. MRI brain (2019) was reported normal. The pattern she describes suggests an increase in susceptibility in the context of disrupted circadian rhythm and insufficient sleep, amounting to a sleep-disruption–linked escalation in events. We discussed practical strategies to improve sleep opportunity around shift work, including protected wind-down time, consistent wake routines post-night shift, and minimising consecutive nights where possible. She will explore temporary adjustments to her rota with occupational health. In view of the recent deterioration, I have recommended we optimise treatment. We will: - Continue levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily for the moment. She will keep a detailed seizure and sleep diary. - Arrange an urgent sleep-deprived EEG and repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol. - Check trough levetiracetam level, vitamin D, and repeat U&E/LFTs. - Provide intranasal midazolam as a rescue plan for prolonged events (>5 minutes) or recurrent episodes within a short period, with partner instruction sheet supplied. I have advised strict sleep hygiene, avoidance of missed doses, and no driving in line with DVLA guidance following recent events. She is aware to seek urgent help if seizures become more frequent, prolonged, or if any injury occurs. I will review her in eight weeks, or sooner if her situation worsens. Seizures now come in flurries over several days, interspersed by brief calmer stretches, i.e. episodic bunching with intervening lulls. Menstrual cycle appears to correlate with the flurries. No new visual aura or focal neurological deficit. No pregnancy plans currently. Examination: Afebrile, pulse 78 regular, BP 116/72. Neurological exam non-focal between events. Weight stable. No rash. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams unremarkable. Investigations: Prior MRI (2021) reported normal. EEG last year: generalised spike–polyspike and wave at 3–4 Hz, photoparoxysmal response. We have requested a repeat EEG given recent deterioration. Sleep fragmentation and heightened anxiety noted. Family have implemented seizure first-aid. Reports memory lapses and word-finding issues after the "bunched" days. Management discussion: We reviewed adherence (she uses a pill organiser; occasional delayed morning dose admitted). Sleep hygiene and illness management reinforced. Safety measures reiterated, including supervision near water and head injury precautions. We discussed medication strategies aligned with generalised epilepsy and her prior adverse effects. She prefers to avoid agents that previously caused significant cognitive slowing. We also discussed non-pharmacological supports (employment adjustments, seizure diary app, and trigger tracking). Potential SUDEP risk factors reviewed sensitively given the current worsening. Plan: - Given the post-viral deterioration and pattern of flurries with brief calm intervals, we will optimise current therapy while awaiting levels and EEG. No immediate new agent added today pending labs, but rescue plan reinforced. - Continue Sodium valproate 600 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily; Clobazam 10 mg nocte to remain for now. If valproate level returns low–mid therapeutic, we may consider careful up-titration; if high, consider adjustment and alternative such as Brivaracetam as a substitution for Levetiracetam if irritability emerges. - Buccal midazolam to be used for convulsions >3 minutes or clusters; family re-trained on use today. - Blood results and EEG to be reviewed within two weeks via telephone clinic; earlier contact if there is another convulsion day or injury. - Work letter provided recommending temporary reduced hours and flexible start times. - DVLA advice reiterated; patient confirms compliance. I am concerned about the recent downturn—particularly the increase in convulsions following the viral illness—and have brought her follow-up forward. Please advise us if you observe further decline or medication issues. She and her partner understand to seek urgent help if events become prolonged, occur back-to-back without recovery, or if there is a significant injury. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Aisha Rahman St Mary’s Hospital Department of Neurology, Praed Street, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Aisha Rahman, Marta Nowak, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H3928476 NHS No. 9012457783 Flat 3, 28 Harrow Road, London, W9 3RJ Diagnoses: Primary generalised epilepsy with occasional catamenial clustering EEG (June 2025): Generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy Current Medication: Sodium valproate 300 mg in the morning and 600 mg at night Folic acid 5 mg once daily Plan: - Continue sodium valproate at current dose; check trough level and LFTs in 3 months - Provide written seizure first-aid and SUDEP advice in preferred language - Refer to epilepsy specialist nurse for care planning and NHS pathway orientation; interpreter to be arranged as needed - Consider perimenstrual dose optimisation or alternative catamenial strategy if breakthrough events persist; to be reviewed after seizure diary review in 4 months - Safety advice: avoid sleep deprivation, limit alcohol, and maintain adherence; no driving in accordance with DVLA guidance until seizure-free for the required period I reviewed Marta Nowak in clinic today with telephone interpreter support. They are a recent migrant to the UK and are still becoming familiar with NHS services and how to obtain repeat prescriptions. We discussed the role of the GP, community pharmacy, and how to contact the neurology team or the epilepsy specialist nurse for advice between appointments. They report a history of generalised seizures beginning in adolescence. Over the past year there have been two brief generalised tonic–clonic seizures, both occurring shortly before menstruation, with preserved recovery and no injuries. Day-to-day, there are intermittent morning myoclonic jerks, especially after poor sleep. A seizure diary kept over the last three months shows a recurring pattern of seizure susceptibility in the late premenstrual window; in their words, "the few days before periods are when things bunch up." There have been no status epilepticus episodes. No red flags for infection or new neurological deficit. Medication adherence is good; no notable adverse effects aside from mild tremor. We discussed risks and benefits of valproate comprehensively, including teratogenicity and the need for highly effective contraception and a Pregnancy Prevention Programme; patient confirms not planning pregnancy and using reliable contraception. Folic acid is continued. Lifestyle measures (sleep regularity and caffeine moderation) have been reinforced. Given the pattern of premenstrual worsening, I have advised continuation of current therapy while we gather more data from the seizure diary to guide any targeted adjustment around the perimenstrual period. If clustering persists, we will consider a limited perimenstrual dose increment or an alternative agent better suited to catamenial exacerbations, balancing efficacy and safety. I will review in 4 months with interpreter support. Blood tests (valproate level, FBC, LFTs) will be arranged via the GP in 2–3 weeks. rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Helen Price Longfield Road Health Centre 12 Longfield Road Bromley Kent BR1 2LF Dear Dr Helen Price Amelia Rhodes, DOB: 03-02-1990, Hospital No: K739512 NHS No. 8472056319 Flat 2, 14 Oakmere Court, Beckenham, BR3 1ST Diagnoses/summary: Focal epilepsy, likely temporal onset, long-standing; patient has practiced aura recognition strategies and is able to describe prodromal symptoms in her own words. She reports that over the past six months she experiences focal aware seizures most weeks, occasionally progressing to focal impaired awareness. She has engaged with structured aura recognition techniques from our epilepsy nurse group and describes her warning features as a "tightness rising in the upper abdomen with a wave of déjà vu and a metallic taste". She is usually able to move to a safe place, silence her phone alerts, and initiate paced breathing when this occurs. Despite these measures, she continues to have intermittent episodes. In terms of medication, she remains on lamotrigine but is unable to increase beyond her current dose due to visual blurring and marked light sensitivity. In effect, up-titration is curtailed by tolerability, and seizures continue at a low-to-moderate frequency. She keeps a diary and shares that sleep loss and missed meals are consistent triggers. No recent injuries. No convulsions for over a year. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 125 mg morning and 150 mg evening - Clobazam 5–10 mg PRN for clusters (no more than 2–3 times per month) - Salbutamol inhaler PRN Lifestyle/safety: She no longer drives and understands DVLA requirements. Plan: We discussed options including adding Zonisamide or Lacosamide, versus optimising behavioural strategies. Given her sensitivity to lamotrigine at higher doses and the ongoing breakthrough events at a dose ceiling, we agreed to a cautious adjunctive trial of Lacosamide. She wishes to proceed. - Start Lacosamide 50 mg nightly for 1 week, then 50 mg twice daily. If tolerated and seizures persist, increase to 100 mg morning and 50 mg evening after 2–3 weeks, with further titration guided by response and side-effects. - Continue Lamotrigine unchanged for now; consider small reductions only if adverse effects increase once Lacosamide is established. - Continue aura recognition and paced-breathing protocol; will provide updated seizure action plan and diary template. - Bloods (U&E, LFT) at 4–6 weeks after reaching 100 mg/day Lacosamide. - Nurse specialist phone review in 4 weeks; clinic review in 3–4 months or sooner if deterioration. Yours sincerely

There are occasional morning headaches and transient myalgia. They do not recall daytime events. They carry a smartphone sleep app which has flagged “restlessness bursts” most nights, particularly between 02:00–04:00. They have installed a basic audio baby monitor; the partner (when present) has previously heard brief groaning and heavy breathing once or twice a week. Overall, the pattern suggests events are clustered during sleep with minimal daytime impact, and the patient reports that day-to-day functioning has been relatively steady with rare interruptions. In practical terms, their current symptom pattern could be described as reasonably steady control in the daytime, with persisting nocturnal episodes under review. He has implemented sleep regularity and reduced alcohol, and his partner reports fewer prolonged postictal phases. He has had no injuries, no emergency department attendances, and no status episodes. He is driving abstinent and adherent to DVLA guidance. Seizure diary review: Focal seizure: 2019: May x0, Jun x0, Jul x1, Aug x0, Sep x1, Oct x2. No tongue laceration or incontinence has been witnessed. rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 29 November 2016 Dr Aisha Khan Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy Kingston Hospital, Galsworthy Road, Kingston upon Thames, KT2 7QB Dear Dr Aisha Khan, Ms Priya Patel, DOB: 24-03-1992, Hospital No: K847301 NHS No. 2039184756 Flat 12, 5 Willow Court, Surbiton, KT6 5NA Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy with probable catamenial pattern; 1 Travel-related clusters this month; ~4 - 6 events per episode Aetiology: No structural lesion identified on MRI; normal perinatal and developmental history; family history notable for a sibling with adolescent-onset generalised seizures Other Medical Problems: Mild iron-deficiency anaemia on oral supplementation; intermittent migraine without aura Management Plan: - Patient has generalised epilepsy with suspected catamenial exacerbation. We reviewed her menstrual tracking app entries which show a consistent increase in events during the late luteal phase and first two days of menses. She also reported 1 Travel-related clusters this month; ~4 - 6 events per episode, temporally associated with early-morning flights and sleep disruption. - Continue Sodium Valproate semi-enteric 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte; maintain single-brand supply. - Introduce perimenstrual rescue strategy: Clobazam 10 mg nocte starting two days before expected menses and continuing for five days, patient-reported and time-limited use; we will review tolerability. - Reinforce sleep hygiene and travel planning: avoid overnight travel where possible; if unavoidable, schedule rest periods and maintain regular dosing times across time zones. - Arrange serum Valproate level, LFTs, FBC, and serum ferritin in four weeks. - Provide letter for employer to support flexible scheduling around long-haul travel weeks. - Safety counselling updated: SUDEP and driving guidance reviewed as per DVLA standards for generalised epilepsy; patient acknowledges understanding. - Follow-up in three months; earlier review if clusters exceed baseline or adverse effects occur. This patient remains otherwise well between episodes with no reported injuries or prolonged post-ictal confusion. App-based logs reviewed in clinic corroborate the cycle-linked increase in frequency and the travel-linked cluster described above. There is no evidence of focal onset features by history or examination today. We discussed medication teratogenicity considerations and contraception; she confirmed ongoing effective contraception and wishes to continue current therapy pending further review. Yours sincerely

They report routine adherence to safety protocols including a protective visor and appropriate shielding. There has been no breach of visor use reported; occasional brief reflections from adjacent bays were noted but without associated symptoms. No sleep deprivation beyond normal shift patterns; hydration and meal timing maintained. Ã‚Â· Minor workplace noise fluctuations reported, but no clear temporal association with neurological events. ï¿½ Present Medication: 1. Tegretol Retard 600 mg twice daily. 2. Ã© Examination/Review Today: Neurological examination unremarkable. No nystagmus, coordination intact, gait steady. Mood stable; no behavioural change on current Keppra dose per patient and partner. rows.note_text: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 01 September 2021 Dr Ahmed St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Ahmed, Sophie Bennett, DOB: 12-03-1992, Hospital No: H583920 NHS No. 9081726345 Flat 3, Rosewood Assisted Living, 14 Brook Street, London, W1K 5DL Medication: Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. Patient-reported adherence is good, with no missed doses in the past month. No adverse effects beyond mild transient irritability in the evenings. Background and supports: The patient resides in assisted living and is supported by a key worker; key-worker notes were reviewed where available. These corroborate stable routines, medication prompts, and no safeguarding concerns. Epilepsy history and current status: This patient has focal epilepsy. Seizures have historically begun with a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest, progressing on occasion to impaired awareness with right-hand automatisms; there have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported in the past year. Last seizure on 31-May, described as a brief focal aware event lasting approximately 20–30 seconds without loss of awareness, occurring in the late afternoon after a disrupted sleep routine. No injuries. Since then, no further events have been recorded by the patient or noted by the key worker. Triggers and lifestyle factors: Patient reports poor sleep and higher work-related stress in late May around the time of the last event. Caffeine intake has been reduced since June and sleep hygiene improved with a consistent bedtime routine, which may have contributed to subsequent stability. Investigations and monitoring: Previous MRI (2019) unremarkable. Routine EEG (2020) showed left temporal intermittent rhythmic activity without definitive epileptiform discharges. No new investigations requested today in view of clinical stability. We have asked the key worker to continue logging any spells of altered awareness or behavioural arrest, and to document potential triggers. Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily unchanged. - Maintain seizure diary (patient and key worker) with attention to sleep, stressors, and any focal aware symptoms. - Safety advice reviewed; no driving. Occupational risk currently low within supervised environment. - Consider repeat EEG only if events recur or evolve. Follow-up: We will review in six months, or sooner if there are further seizures or concerning changes. Yours sincerely
