rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 04 September 2024 Dr Patel St George's Hospital Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Sophie Williams, DOB: 14-07-1992, Hospital No: H629514 NHS No. 8473629150 12 Brookside Avenue, London, SW12 8JP Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation. I reviewed Sophie Williams in clinic today accompanied by her partner. She has been practising aura recognition strategies as previously discussed and was able to describe her typical warnings in her own words. She reports a rising epigastric sensation, a metallic taste, and a brief sense of detachment lasting 10–20 seconds, which she identifies as her focal aware phase. She has been using these early symptoms to alert others and to move to a safe position, which she feels has reduced injury risk. There has been little alteration in seizure frequency over the past year; she experiences one to two generalised tonic-clonic seizures monthly with the longest seizure-free period being three weeks. She has 4 absences per day. In addition, she suffers clusters of myoclonic jerks and occasional tonic seizures, these occur roughly once a month. No seizures have been recorded since her last appointment. She keeps a detailed seizure diary and has linked increased events with poor sleep and missed meals. She denies recent head injury, new medications, or intercurrent illness. No ambulance call-outs, emergency department attendances, or injuries have occurred since we last met. Current anti-seizure medications are unchanged per patient report. She continues to use a smartphone reminder for doses and her partner confirms adherence. She has not required rescue medication since the previous visit. There is no implanted neuromodulation device in situ. On examination today she was alert and orientated, with normal speech and language. Cranial nerves, coordination, power, sensation, and gait were unremarkable. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were within normal limits. We discussed ongoing self-management with particular emphasis on prompt response to auras, maintaining regular sleep and meals, and continuing the diary. She is aware of SUDEP information and first aid measures. We agreed to continue current management and to monitor for any evolution of her focal symptoms or change in seizure semiology. She will contact the service sooner if she notes prolonged clusters, injuries, or any adverse effects from medication. Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure therapy as tolerated. - Persist with aura recognition strategies and safety planning as practised. - Maintain seizure diary including potential triggers, duration, and recovery. - Routine follow-up in 4 months, or earlier if clinical change occurs. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 27 July 2014 10:15 To: neuro.clinic@nhs.net Cc: Dr Michael O’Neill (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Clinic review and study-period considerations Hi Emily Background: The patient is a university student approaching end-of-term examinations and reports prolonged study hours with irregular sleep and meal patterns. Most of the history today is patient-reported; no collateral informant was available. She has used a study and seizure diary app intermittently since her last visit. Epilepsy Diagnosis: Type not specified. Present Medication: 1. Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily (self-reported full adherence; pharmacy refills consistent) 2. Clobazam 10 mg at night (taken on most nights; occasionally omitted due to morning grogginess per patient) 3. Folic acid 5 mg once daily Present Seizure Frequency: There has been little alteration in seizure frequency over the past year; she experiences one to two generalised tonic-clonic seizures monthly with the longest seizure-free period being three weeks. She has 4 absences per day. In addition, she suffers clusters of myoclonic jerks and occasional tonic seizures, these occur roughly once a month. No seizures have been recorded since her last appointment. Relevant Context Since Last Review: - She reports that examination preparation has led to sleep restriction (averaging 5–6 hours/night) and increased caffeine intake (3–4 coffees/day), with occasional missed meals. She perceives sleep loss as a possible trigger for events historically. - No recent intercurrent illness, alcohol intake minimal, and no recreational drug use reported. - She has not yet completed the requested seizure safety e-learning but has read the paper leaflet provided at the last visit. - No injuries since last visit; no emergency department attendances in the interim. Investigations/Monitoring: - No new investigations since the previous review. The last EEG and MRI results are unchanged from prior records. She is open to ambulatory EEG if scheduling permits outside exam weeks. - She has kept a partial seizure diary; we encouraged consistent daily entries, particularly across the examination period. Plan of Action: - Maintain current anti-seizure medications unchanged until after the examination period to avoid destabilisation. We discussed that any medication adjustments will be considered at the next review when academic pressures ease. - Non-pharmacological measures (patient-reported goals): prioritise regular sleep routine (target 7–8 hours), moderate caffeine use, maintain regular meals and hydration, and continue diary logging of events, sleep duration, and potential triggers. - Safety reminders reinforced: avoid unsupervised swimming/bathing, use a shower where possible, and consider the student disability service for examination adjustments (e.g., rest breaks, separate room). She will liaise with her university’s wellbeing team. - We provided a written plan for managing potential clusters of myoclonic jerks during the study period and when to seek urgent care (prolonged events >5 minutes, repeated events without recovery, or injury). - Follow-up arranged in 4 months, with an interim telephone check-in in 6–8 weeks. She will contact the clinic sooner if there is a sustained change in seizure pattern, adverse effects, or concerns regarding study-related stress. With best wishes

rows.note_text: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Ahmed Maple Road Surgery 12 Maple Road, Harrow, London HA3 7QT Dear Dr Ahmed, Sophie Bennett, DOB: 14-02-1993, Hospital No: N483920 NHS No. 9081726453 22 Brookside Close, Harrow, London HA2 6LN Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy Medication: • Lamotrigine 150 mg morning / 200 mg evening • Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily Thank you for reviewing this patient who has a confirmed history of generalised epilepsy. Over the past six months seizure control has been stable; she suffers one generalised tonic-clonic seizure every 3 months, with a maximum seizure-free period of four weeks. Weekly absences persist. She also experiences atonic seizures and focal seizures with impaired awareness, each arising once every few months. Since the last visit, she has not had any reported episodes. Despite the above stable numerical pattern, she reports a concerning qualitative deterioration. Specifically, her aura characteristics have changed with more rapid evolution into impaired awareness, and she notes a shorter prodrome and increased sensory distortion preceding events. The auras are now briefer and progress more quickly, particularly in the late afternoon and with sleep deprivation. She also reports greater post-ictal confusion and headache compared to prior baseline. There have been no injuries, but she has required assistance at work on two occasions due to prolonged recovery. She remains fully adherent to lamotrigine and levetiracetam and denies missed doses. No intercurrent illness or alcohol excess. Menses are regular and there is no clear catamenial pattern. She has been undertaking longer shifts, and sleep has been reduced to approximately 5–6 hours on several weekdays, which may be contributory. There is no new medication or supplement use. Examination in clinic today was non-focal and unchanged. Routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) from last month were within normal limits per patient report; we have requested copies for our records. She has not yet undergone the repeat EEG we previously suggested; we have re-booked this to evaluate for any evolution in interictal generalised spike–wave activity. Given the altered aura phenomenology with more rapid evolution, we regard this as a deterioration in her condition despite the apparent stability of event counts. We discussed lifestyle regularisation, seizure first aid, and maintaining a seizure diary with specific attention to aura onset, duration, and precipitating factors. She is fit to continue current duties with caution and agreed workplace adjustments around rest breaks. Driving status was reviewed in accordance with DVLA guidance; she understands her obligations to report and to cease driving if criteria are not met. Plan: • Continue lamotrigine 150 mg AM / 200 mg PM and levetiracetam 1000 mg BD unchanged for now while we reassess. • Arrange early EEG and consider ambulatory recording if routine study is non-diagnostic. • Repeat serum lamotrigine level for reference (non-urgent). • Follow-up in the neurology clinic in 8–10 weeks or sooner if escalation occurs (e.g., injuries, clustering, or prolonged post-ictal states). We will keep you updated following investigations. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 23 April 2014 Dr Amelia Kerr St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Amelia Kerr, Michael Turner, DOB: 14-02-1987, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 9031142286 27 Brookfield Close, Mitcham, CR4 1QX Diagnoses: Recurrent unprovoked seizures under investigation; prior normal brain MRI (February 2014). rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 22 January 2017 Dr Amelia Rhodes Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Amelia Rhodes Consultant Neurologist, Mr Peter Langley, DOB: 14-03-1954, Hospital No: KCH782411 NHS No. 9473165820 Flat 2, 18 Rowan Court, Dulwich, London SE21 8JT Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in the neurology clinic today. He is a newly retired teacher who lives alone, maintains a regular daily routine, and reports reduced social contact since retirement. He attended unaccompanied and was able to give a clear account of his history. He describes two distinct seizure types consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The focal events begin with a rising epigastric sensation and a brief pause with loss of awareness, during which he is noted to stare and fumble with nearby objects for up to 60–90 seconds, followed by several minutes of confusion. Separately, he has generalised tonic–clonic seizures that typically occur from sleep or in the early morning without a clear prodrome. There is no consistent trigger identified, though he reports that missed meals and fragmented sleep have occasionally preceded events. Following introduction of lamotrigine, there has been a clear improvement in control, with just nine generalised tonic-clonic seizures documented this year to date. He also reports a reduction in the frequency of focal impaired-awareness episodes, now occurring roughly once every three to four weeks, usually clustering after periods of stress or disrupted sleep. He keeps a written seizure diary, which correlates with this history. There is no history of status epilepticus. Post-ictally he experiences myalgia and headache for several hours, but there is no prolonged confusion beyond the immediate recovery period. He denies tongue-biting outside of the generalised events and has had two minor falls this year without injury. There is no current use of alcohol or recreational drugs, and he remains independent with activities of daily living. He has limited social contact but is open to community support should it be available. Current anti-seizure medication is lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, well tolerated without rash, dizziness, or diplopia. He is not on any other anti-seizure therapy at present, and there have been no recent medication changes. He is adherent and uses a pill organiser. Sleep hygiene is reasonable; he typically retires at 22:30 and rises at 06:30. On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal language, intact cranial nerves, normal tone and power throughout, symmetrical reflexes, and a normal gait. There were no focal neurological deficits detected. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. In summary, the clinical picture is of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, with both focal impaired-awareness seizures and separate generalised tonic–clonic seizures. Seizure control has improved on lamotrigine, with a clear reduction in generalised events this year as above. We discussed ongoing risk reduction, including consistent sleep routine, regular meals, and maintaining the seizure diary. He is not currently driving and understands DVLA guidance as applicable. I have provided information on local peer support groups to address social isolation, which he welcomed. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; no immediate dose change given current benefit and tolerability. - Arrange routine EEG and updated MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to further characterise both generalised and focal features. - Check lamotrigine trough level, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, and vitamin D at next phlebotomy. - Reinforce seizure diary and safety advice at home; provide written advice on when to seek urgent care. - Follow-up in clinic in 6 months, or sooner should there be any deterioration or clustering of seizures. Thank you for your referral. Please do not hesitate to contact me if any issues arise before the next appointment. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 20 May 2024 Dr Aisha Rahman Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy King’s College Hospital, Denmark Hill, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Aisha Rahman, Mr Thomas Green, DOB: 22-09-1987, Hospital No: K7845129 NHS No. 9432175068 Flat 12, 45 Station Parade, London, NW5 4HT Diagnosis: Recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain classification; current working diagnosis remains under review pending further corroborative data. Aetiology: No definitive structural, genetic, or metabolic cause identified to date. Brain MRI (March 2024) reported normal. Routine EEG (February 2024) non-specific without clear epileptiform discharges. Other Medical Problems: Mild intermittent low back pain attributed to prolonged standing at work; seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with as-needed non-sedating antihistamine. Management Plan: Continue Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily. Reinforce adherence and single-brand prescribing to minimise variability. Arrange extended ambulatory EEG with video (72-hour) to capture habitual events. Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, Lamotrigine trough level. Provide updated workplace letter outlining safety considerations around crowd surges, heat stress, and sleep disruption. Review in four months; sooner if breakthrough seizures occur or adverse effects emerge. Since our last appointment, the patient and family report improved overall control. The family feel seizure frequency has decreased markedly since starting medication, with only five seizures so far this year. Events remain brief (30–60 seconds) with rapid recovery, typically preceded by a sense of internal "rush" and occasional lip-smacking noted by relatives. No clear precipitants, though episodes have clustered after consecutive early shifts and during exceptionally busy gate-line periods with crowd surges. No injuries reported. He has self-restricted lone ladder use and heavy manual coupling tasks during early mornings. We discussed occupational risk in the context of his role at a busy metro station gate line, where prolonged standing, fluctuating temperatures, and crowd dynamics can be fatiguing. I have advised practical measures: maintaining regular breaks where service permits, hydration, avoidance of missed meals, prioritising consistent sleep, and avoiding lone work in high-risk areas. He will liaise with his manager regarding rota patterns to limit consecutive early starts and to ensure a colleague is present during peak crowd surges. DVLA guidance has been reviewed; he confirms ongoing compliance and will notify us immediately of any change in frequency or severity. He denies rash, mood change, or notable cognitive side effects on Lamotrigine. Occasional dizziness reported when dehydrated on hot platforms; we discussed countermeasures. No current plans for dose escalation given improved control and tolerability; future adjustments will be guided by seizure diary, levels, and ambulatory EEG findings. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 24 January 2015 Dr Alison Green Riverside Medical Practice 14 Wren Street, London WC1X 0BP Dear Dr Alison Green, Daniel Carter, DOB: 22-08-1978, Hospital No: C784210 NHS No. 3015529476 Flat 3, 29 Brookfield Road, London E9 5AL Summary/ Diagnoses: History of seizures of uncertain classification; type 2 diabetes managed in primary care; dyspepsia; intermittent low mood under GP review; ex-smoker. Medication: - Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. - Carbamazepine modified release 400 mg twice daily. - Metformin 1 g twice daily. - Omeprazole 20 mg once daily. - Sertraline 50 mg once daily. I reviewed him in clinic today accompanied by his mother, who provides most collateral history between appointments. He reports good general health and regular meals, and his mother confirms that medication adherence has been reliable with a weekly pill organiser. No recent intercurrent illnesses. He denies alcohol or recreational drugs. Sleep has been variable but improving with a consistent bedtime routine; he is engaging in short daily walks. Capillary glucose monitoring is performed in primary care; he did not bring a log today but recalls recent readings typically between 6–9 mmol/L fasting. He has not experienced hypoglycaemia symptoms. Weight is stable by report. Seizures: His mother notes an overall improvement compared with previous years, with four tonic seizures documented in 2015 so far. These have occurred without clear provocation according to the family diary. There is no reported prolonged postictal confusion, tongue biting, or injury this year. No witnessed episodes suggestive of status epilepticus. He is keeping a simple calendar-based record at home which I have encouraged them to continue bringing to clinic. Examination: He was alert and oriented with fluent speech. Cranial nerves intact. Motor power full with normal tone and coordination; no lateralising signs. Gait normal. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. No peripheral stigmata of vascular disease. Diabetes: Managed by the GP team; no neuropathic symptoms volunteered and foot inspection today showed intact skin and normal capillary refill. I have reiterated the importance of annual retinal screening and routine HbA1c monitoring in primary care. Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure medication regimen without change. - Reinforce seizure diary completion and bring copies to next review. - Safety: advised standard precautions including supervised bathing and avoiding heights; driving not applicable as he does not hold a licence. - Liaise with practice to ensure HbA1c and lipids are up to date; defer diabetes medication management to primary care. - Arrange follow-up in neurology clinic in six months, or earlier if there is any increase in seizure frequency, new injury, or prolonged events. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 25 May 2016 Dr James Rowe Centre for Epilepsy Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr James Rowe, Daniel Harper, DOB: 22-11-1992, Hospital No: H673920 NHS No. 9842157630 Flat 3, 47 Merton Road, London SW18 5JY Focal Epilepsy Occupation and context: Works as a line cook in a commercial kitchen, with prolonged shifts at high heat, frequent exposure to flashing heat lamps, and rapid task transitions. Events occur in the kitchen during service. Medication: Patient-reported current regimen includes carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily started February 2016; using buccal midazolam 10 mg as rescue per workplace protocol (kept in manager’s office, not used to date). No known adverse drug reactions reported today aside from occasional mild dizziness at the end of long evening shifts. Carbamazepine Blood Level: 18 May 2016: 6.8 mg/L (laboratory reference 4–12 mg/L). Dose 200 mg twice daily at time of sample. Seizures and semiology: The patient has focal epilepsy. Typical focal impaired-awareness events begin with a rising epigastric sensation and metallic taste, followed by behavioural arrest, right-hand automatisms, and brief non-responsiveness lasting 45–60 seconds, with post-event fatigue of approximately 15 minutes. Events have been witnessed by colleagues under heat lamps on the pass during peak service. His mother notes an overall improvement compared with previous years, with eight tonic seizures documented in 2016 so far. These tonic events have been brief (under 30 seconds) and occurred after clusters of focal episodes on exceptionally hot, high-stress evenings; no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported this year. No reported auras preceding the tonic events; focal auras persist prior to impaired-awareness episodes. Workplace factors: Dehydration risk acknowledged; he now carries electrolyte drinks and rotates away from the grill when prodromal symptoms occur, per manager support. Staff are aware of the rescue plan and recovery position protocol. No injuries sustained; one near-miss with a hot pan was avoided by colleague intervention. Investigations: Prior MRI (2014) reportedly normal; routine EEG (2015) showed left temporal intermittent rhythmic slowing without definite epileptiform discharges (patient report; formal report not to hand today). Plan discussed today by telephone review with patient and his mother present: - Continue carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily; adherence emphasised with dosing after pre-shift meal and at bedtime to minimise dizziness during service. - Maintain hydration and scheduled brief cool-down breaks as agreed with employer. - Rescue buccal midazolam to remain accessible; no use to date. - Request copy of prior MRI/EEG and consider repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to better characterise focal onset if events persist. - Safety: continue heat-exposure precautions, avoid carrying heavy pans when aura occurs, and ensure a colleague escorts him off the line during episodes. - Review in 3 months or earlier if frequency increases or injuries occur. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 24 March 2017 Dr Emily Carter Riverside Medical Practice 12 Wharf Street, London, SE1 3AB Dear Dr Emily Carter Michael Turner, DOB: 08-02-1979, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 7482910365 Mooring 27, South Dock Marina, London, SE16 7SZ I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He has a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, with events described as focal seizures with impaired awareness (often starting with a metallic taste and right-hand posturing) and separate generalised tonic–clonic seizures sometimes occurring from sleep. Following introduction of lamotrigine, there has been a clear improvement in control, with just seven generalised tonic-clonic seizures documented this year to date. He also reports brief focal events approximately once every 2–3 weeks, usually clustering after poor sleep or during periods when his device alarms cannot be charged due to power interruptions. Current treatment is lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. and levetiracetam 1 g b.d. He reports good adherence and no rash, dizziness, or visual disturbance. Mild insomnia is noted, which he associates with variable noise from the marina; he does not drink alcohol and consumes one coffee each morning. No recent head injuries. There is no family history of epilepsy to his knowledge. Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable. No cognitive complaints beyond occasional word-finding difficulty after nocturnal seizures. We reviewed safety: he avoids heights and swimming alone, and uses a kettle with auto shut-off. He has a smartphone seizure diary; I advised continuing entries and photographing any tongue biting or injuries for documentation. He is aware of DVLA regulations and confirms he is not driving. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. and levetiracetam 1 g b.d. given the improved generalised seizure control. - Arrange routine EEG to further characterise interictal abnormalities in the context of combined generalised and focal features, and repeat serum lamotrigine level pre-morning dose in 8 weeks. - Provide written advice on sleep hygiene and strategies for managing power outages (portable battery pack for phone and alarm device; patient to consider). This was framed as patient choice. - Follow-up in 4 months, sooner if seizure frequency increases or adverse effects emerge. I will update you after the EEG and blood results. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 22 May 2020 Dr Amelia Hart Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Amelia Hart Consultant Neurologist, Daniel Fraser, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K917204 NHS No. 7482309156 19 Westbrook Lane, London, SE15 2QJ Thank you for your referral and for the accompanying summary. I reviewed Daniel Fraser in clinic today. He describes a history consistent with focal epilepsy, with events typically beginning with a right temporal aura (rising epigastric sensation and brief déjà vu) followed by behavioural arrest and lip-smacking, occasionally progressing to impaired awareness. There has been a steady improvement over recent months. Sleep hygiene measures have been implemented reliably, and his routine bedtime and wake time are now consistent; his partner also reports that the pattern of events appears more stable. Since optimising Brivaracetam and reinforcing sleep routines, the family report that episodes have become noticeably fewer; to characterise it in their words, they feel the seizures have tailed off substantially this year, with only a small handful recorded so far. He is keeping a seizure diary which corroborates this trend and shows longer seizure-free intervals, particularly over the last 10 weeks. Semiology remains focal: preserved posture with brief unresponsiveness, oroalimentary automatisms, and post-event confusion lasting 10–15 minutes, without prolonged agitation. There have been no clearly documented nocturnal convulsions. He denies new neurological deficits, and there is no evidence of interictal psychosis or mood disorder at present. He and his partner both feel more confident managing triggers; caffeine has been reduced and adherence to medication is excellent by pill count. Impression: Focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset, with improving control on current regimen. The overall trajectory is favourable, with better sleep hygiene and a stabilised daily routine likely contributing to fewer events and a more predictable pattern. Plan: - Continue Brivaracetam at current dose; no change today given ongoing improvement. - Maintain sleep schedule and seizure diary to document frequency and potential precipitants. - Safety advice reinforced (showers rather than baths, avoid sleep deprivation, and continue partner-supervised early night routine). - Routine bloods for antiepileptic drug safety monitoring locally via GP in 3 months. - Telephone review in 3 months, earlier if breakthrough events increase or new features arise. Thank you again for your helpful letter and ongoing care. Please do not hesitate to contact me if there are any concerns. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 21 January 2021 Dr Amelia Hart St George’s University Hospital Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Amelia Hart, Thomas Green, DOB: 14-03-1992, Hospital No: G473920 NHS No. 9065412378 12 Brookfield Avenue, Tooting, London SW17 8AB Diagnoses: - Focal epilepsy with probable left temporal onset, adult presentation with history of childhood febrile seizures. - MRI brain (December 2020): Subtle left mesial temporal T2/FLAIR signal change without definite volume loss. - EEG (November 2020): Left temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity with occasional sharp waves. I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He is a university student approaching end-of-term examinations and reports long study hours with variable sleep, particularly over the last month. He described episodic brief inattentive spells over several years, often during periods of academic stress, though these have not been formally witnessed by clinicians. He remained seizure-free for seven months after starting Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, before experiencing a generalised tonic-clonic seizure 3 Tuesdays ago, preceded by a cluster of absences. The convulsive event lasted approximately 90 seconds per collateral history from a friend, followed by post-ictal confusion and myalgia for several hours. There was no reported tongue bite or urinary incontinence. He did not miss any medication doses in the week preceding the event but had slept 4–5 hours nightly for several nights and had consumed significant caffeine. On examination today, general and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Vital signs were stable. There are no known precipitants beyond sleep deprivation and high caffeine intake as reported by the patient. There is no history of febrile convulsions, CNS infection, or significant head injury. Family history is non-contributory by his account. We discussed the importance of consistent sleep, hydration, and meal timing, especially during examination periods. I have advised continuation of Levetiracetam at the current dose, given overall tolerability (he reports mild irritability that has improved with regular meals and structured breaks). He agrees to continue a detailed seizure diary, including potential triggers, with video capture if safe to obtain. I will arrange EEG and MRI brain to aid further assessment. He is aware of DVLA regulations and understands the need to refrain from driving as per current guidance following the recent event. He has asked for a letter to his university to support reasonable adjustments during exams; I will provide this. I will review him in 3 months, or sooner via our advice line if there are further seizures or any concerns about adverse effects. With best wishes,

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 6 May 2025 Dr Patel St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Michael Roberts, DOB: 14-02-1989, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 8472395610 Moorings 12, Regent’s Canal, London, NW1 8AL Diagnoses: Recurrent unprovoked seizures; aetiology and electroclinical classification currently unclear. Thank you for asking me to review Michael Roberts in clinic today. The history below is patient-reported. He lives on a houseboat/mobile home and reports occasional power outages that intermittently affect charging of his wearable seizure-alert device and phone. He is not currently using a VNS or other implanted neuromodulation. There have been no recent hospital admissions for seizures. No new injuries reported. Seizure history and current pattern: - Seizures in 2024-2025: Aug: 6 days, most of them at sleep time, Sep: 11 days with seizures, Oct: 1 days, Nov: 7 days, most of them at sleep time, Dec: 8 days with seizures Jan: 9 days, Feb: 8 days with seizures Mar: 2 days. He describes events as sudden loss of awareness with stiffening followed by shaking in some episodes, and in others a brief behavioural arrest with blank staring; occasional tongue biting noted on waking. Post-event fatigue can last several hours. He estimates most events in August and November occurred during sleep. He does not drive. Medications: - Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily (self-reported; adherence occasionally impacted when charging reminders fail during power cuts). - Buccal midazolam is not held; no recent emergency rescue therapy used. Investigations and monitoring: - Prior routine EEG (2023) reportedly normal per patient; formal report not available to review today. - No recent MRI brain available in our system; patient believes an MRI was performed elsewhere several years ago. - No device diagnostics applicable as he does not have an implanted system. Assessment: The reported frequency shows variability month to month with several nocturnal events. History is patient-reported and partially limited by lack of contemporaneous records and intermittent disruption of digital seizure logging due to power outages on the houseboat. There is no clear precipitant identified. Further classification remains pending correlation with investigations. Plan agreed today: - Request prior EEG and MRI reports from external providers; if not obtainable, arrange repeat MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) and sleep-deprived EEG. - Provide a paper seizure diary as backup when devices cannot be charged; reinforce timestamping of events and any potential triggers. - Check lamotrigine trough level and routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC). - Discussed SUDEP information and nocturnal seizure safety; provided written advice. - Community epilepsy nurse to contact patient regarding strategies for medication adherence during power outages. - Follow-up in 3 months or sooner if events escalate, injuries occur, or prolonged episodes develop. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 14 September 2025 Dr Priya Desai King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Priya Desai, Daniel Carter, DOB: 17-03-1982, Hospital No: KCH902311 NHS No. 9483726150 12 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 2HQ Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in clinic today with his partner. He described a long history of intermittent episodes that have varied over the years. The current concerns relate to brief spells of behavioural arrest with a sense of pressure in the chest and a tendency to pace or fidget, usually lasting a few minutes, without clear loss of awareness, and without tongue biting or incontinence. He can feel unsettled afterwards but returns to baseline within 10–15 minutes. He has not reported injuries or nocturnal events in recent months. He had previously been referred after a period of frequent episodes during a stressful time at work. Since engaging with psychological support and using relaxation techniques advised by our liaison psychology team, his day-to-day anxiety has eased. In that context, events at present are considered non-epileptic and have become more manageable now that his anxiety is better controlled. He and his partner keep a simple diary which shows fewer episodes over the past six weeks, and they both feel more confident about identifying triggers and using breathing strategies early. There is no clear history to suggest a specific seizure phenotype, and prior routine EEG and MRI from last year were unremarkable. He remains on a stable dose of Brivaracetam initiated previously by another service; he has not had adverse effects and prefers no change at this stage. We discussed the potential value of further characterisation should the picture alter, including ambulatory EEG or admission for video-EEG telemetry if clinically indicated, but for now he is content to continue with self-management and follow-up. On examination today, he was oriented, with normal speech and language, and no focal neurological deficits. Mood appeared steadier than at his last review according to his partner. There were no red flags suggestive of acute risk. Plan: - Continue current medication without adjustment at present. - Maintain psychological strategies and the episode diary; they will record context, duration, and recovery features. - Safety advice reinforced, including avoidance of high-risk situations during episodes. - Open access to clinic if the pattern changes, new features emerge (loss of awareness, injuries, nocturnal events), or frequency escalates. - Routine review in 4–6 months, sooner if needed. Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are any concerns you would like us to address in the interim. Yours sincerely,

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Amelia Hart Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Amelia Hart Consultant Neurologist, Sarah Thompson, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH482917 NHS No. 9876543210 12 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 3AB Thank you for asking me to review your patient in the neurology clinic. She attended with her partner. We discussed her known generalised epilepsy and a recent pattern of events she has been recording in a diary, including notes about mood and irritability prior to some episodes. History and current status: She reports a longstanding diagnosis of generalised epilepsy, initially established in adolescence with typical generalised tonic–clonic seizures and occasional brief absences. Over the past year she has had two generalised convulsions, both in the context of sleep deprivation. In addition, she has experienced intermittent brief spells of subjective “rising tension”, irritability, and tearfulness over several hours that sometimes culminate in a short period of staring and loss of awareness without convulsion. She and her partner have carefully tracked these in a diary; the mood change often precedes the events by 12–24 hours. Since improving sleep routine and stress management, the seizure-like spells have settled considerably. At present, the seizure-like episodes appear to be non-epileptic in character and have become less intrusive as her general wellbeing has improved. Her last definite generalised tonic–clonic seizure was four months ago. Epilepsy type: She has generalised epilepsy. There is no history suggestive of focal onset. Prior EEG (per patient report, 2021) showed generalised spike–wave discharges. There is no head injury history or alcohol misuse. Medication: She is currently taking sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. No missed doses reported in the past three months. She uses folic acid as advised. No rashes, weight stable, mild irritability that she correlates with work stress rather than medication. Examination: Normal bedside neurological examination. No focal deficits. Cardiovascular and respiratory observations unremarkable. Assessment: Generalised epilepsy with infrequent generalised tonic–clonic seizures, and additional diary-documented episodes featuring prodromal mood change and irritability that are currently felt to be non-epileptic and improved in parallel with better sleep and reduced stress. The diary has been very helpful in delineating triggers and temporal patterns. Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure medications unchanged for now. - Continue seizure and mood diary, specifically noting sleep duration, stressors, and menstrual cycle where relevant. - Provide SUDEP and safety advice as discussed today (including driving and water safety). - Arrange routine EEG to reassess background where feasible and bloods for anti-seizure medication levels and bone health. - Offer referral to clinical psychology for strategies around stress, sleep hygiene, and managing premonitory mood changes; she is open to this. Follow-up: Review in clinic in six months, or sooner if she experiences further generalised seizures or any change in pattern. Please let me know if you would like any further information. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 10 January 2023 Dr Patel St. George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Blackshaw Road, Tooting, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Thomas Reed, DOB: 14-08-1988, Hospital No: H529476 NHS No. 9483726150 12 Brookside Close, Wimbledon, London SW19 3AX Diagnoses: Seizure disorder. Thank you for reviewing Thomas Reed, who attended clinic today with his partner. Over the past six weeks there has been a notable deterioration in his overall stability, with several recent events associated with falls or minor injuries reported at home and outdoors. He describes escalating post-ictal confusion and bruising to the knees and forearms following two unwitnessed collapses on stairs and when exiting public transport. He has not required emergency treatment, but these occurrences have increased his and his partner’s anxiety regarding safety and supervision. Medication and recent course: He came off Levetiracetam on 10 December. In the following week, he had several seizures, one associated with sleep deprivation. No further seizures have occurred since. He reports that sleep quality has been variable and that he occasionally misses meals when working late. No other anti-seizure medicines are currently prescribed, and there have been no recent intercurrent illnesses. He is using a smartphone seizure diary, which corroborates the timing of the early post-withdrawal events and the subsequent seizure-free interval. Examination today was unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory observations and no focal neurological deficit. Gait was steady during assessment, though he remains apprehensive about uneven surfaces following the recent falls. There are fading ecchymoses on the left forearm and right patella without joint effusion. Investigations and management plan: We discussed risk minimisation given the recent deterioration in functional safety. I advised practical measures around sleep regularity, hydration, and avoidance of alcohol excess; he has agreed to implement these. A community occupational therapy falls assessment has been requested to review his home environment (stairs lighting, bathroom rails) and street safety. I have arranged an ambulatory EEG and updated bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D) to exclude contributory factors. We will also obtain a repeat MRI (epilepsy protocol) given the step-change in injury pattern, even though there has been no definitive new neurological sign. We have provided a work note recommending temporary modification of duties to reduce lone working at height and to allow scheduled rest breaks. He and his partner have been counselled on immediate first aid measures and timing of emergency escalation should further collapses occur. He has been given a written safety plan and instructed to continue the seizure diary. Follow-up: I will review him in six weeks or sooner if further seizures or injuries occur. If the falls persist or if there is any recurrence of seizures, we will reconsider initiation of anti-seizure medication after discussing options and potential side effects at that time. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 14 August 2021 Dr Patel Riverside Neurology Clinic 12 Riverbank Way, London SE10 3AB Dear Dr Patel, Marie Dupont, DOB: 14-06-1989, Hospital No: H6723105 NHS No. 9087453216 Flat 3, 27 Oakfield Terrace, London W6 4JD Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy. Thank you for reviewing Marie Dupont, who attended today with her partner. She is the primary caregiver for her young children and reports that night-time sleep can be interrupted, which has made nocturnal monitoring challenging. She experienced her first seizure in January 2021 while on holiday in Spain. It occurred in the early morning hours. She described sudden stiffness in both legs. Her second and third seizure was in July 2021 back home in France, again during sleep, lasting around three minutes with the same clinical features. Since July there have been no further events reported. The events are clinically consistent with focal seizures, likely arising from a frontal network given the brief, predominantly motor semiology during sleep. There is no history of tongue biting, incontinence, or prolonged post-ictal confusion. She has not required emergency rescue medication. There is no prior history of epilepsy, head injury, CNS infection, or perinatal complications. Family history is negative for seizures. Current medications: none. She does not use alcohol to excess and reports no recreational drug use. Caffeine intake is modest, though sleep disruption related to childcare remains a potential trigger. Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Investigations: We have organised an MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and an outpatient sleep-deprived EEG to better characterise focal onset. Routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, glucose) have been requested. Management plan: - Provisional diagnosis of focal epilepsy pending investigation results. We discussed treatment options and have agreed to defer antiseizure medication initiation unless further events occur or investigations show high-risk features; the patient prefers this approach given the limited seizure count and nocturnal occurrence. - Safety advice provided regarding nocturnal supervision, avoiding sleep deprivation where possible, and general seizure first aid for the family. Driving regulations were discussed and she confirms she is not currently driving. - We will review after investigations in approximately 8 weeks, or sooner if further seizures occur. She has a direct contact number for the epilepsy nurse specialist. Yours sincerely,

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 14 November 2014 Dr James Hart Centre for Epilepsy Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr James Hart, Robert Keller, DOB: 22-03-1982, Hospital No: H3849201 NHS No. 9384756102 Flat 5, 27 Marlborough Road, London, N19 4HT Epilepsy Medication: Post-operative prophylaxis with Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily since late October 2014; now tapering to 250 mg twice daily over the next 2 weeks as discussed in MDT. No adverse effects reported. Anti-seizure Drug Levels: Not clinically indicated at present. Routine U&Es and LFTs within normal limits on 10 November 2014. Seizures: His initial event was in July 2014 in Germany, arising from sleep. He awoke with jerking of the left arm and facial twitching. A second event occurred in Italy the following October 2014, once more during the night, lasting four minutes with similar semiology. He has had no further events since surgical intervention and initiation of Levetiracetam. History and Progress: I reviewed Robert Keller today in follow-up after a right temporal surgical procedure performed in late October 2014 abroad, with operative notes confirming a well-circumscribed lesion resected. He reports marked improvement: uninterrupted sleep, no nocturnal motor activity witnessed by his partner, and return to light work duties without cognitive complaints. Headache and incision discomfort have settled; there is no photophobia or phonophobia. Neurological examination today is normal, including facial symmetry and limb power. He remains medically fit to continue graded return to normal activity. We have discussed typical post-operative triggers; he is maintaining good sleep hygiene and reducing caffeine. Plan: - Continue Levetiracetam 250 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then stop if seizure-free and well; he understands to contact the service immediately if any further events occur. - Community nurse to check wound site next week as routine. - DVLA guidance discussed; he is aware of current restrictions and will refrain from driving until permitted. - Telephone review in 6 weeks, face-to-face if any recurrence or concerns. Overall Impression: Clinical course is improving following surgery, with no recurrence of nocturnal motor events and steady functional recovery. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 14 June 2024 Dr R Patel St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Atkinson Morley Wing, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr R Patel, Michael O’Connor, DOB: 14-08-1994, Hospital No: H928374 NHS No. 9074526311 12 Rowan Mews, Flat 3, London, SW11 2BQ Diagnoses: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy). Thank you for referring Michael O’Connor for pre-conception counselling. He attended clinic today with his partner. We reviewed his seizure history, current management, and considerations for pregnancy planning from a paternal perspective, including medication safety, driving, safety planning, and genetic counselling information. Seizure history and semiology: - His first seizure occurred in January 2024 in Ireland, at night while asleep. He woke with rhythmic twitching of the right arm and a sense of déjà vu. The second and third event was in June 2024 in Scotland, also during sleep, lasting five minutes with a similar pattern of symptoms. - He also reports two lifetime episodes (both in 2023) of brief generalised myoclonic jerks on awakening after sleep deprivation, without loss of awareness, and one episode of probable generalised tonic–clonic seizure in adolescence after heavy alcohol intake (no medical review at the time). - Triggers identified: sleep deprivation and excess alcohol. No history of status epilepticus. Investigations to date: - MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) May 2024: no focal cortical dysplasia or hippocampal sclerosis identified; structurally normal study. - EEG April 2024: intermittent left temporal sharp waves during drowsiness; generalised 3–4 Hz spike–wave bursts provoked by hyperventilation, consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. - Routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, B12/folate, glucose) April 2024: within reference range. Current treatment: - He is not yet on anti-seizure medication (ASM). We discussed first-line options suitable for combined generalised and focal epilepsy. Given his seizure recurrence during sleep and mixed generalised/focal features, broad-spectrum ASMs were reviewed. He wishes to defer immediate initiation pending further counselling, safety planning, and confirmation of pregnancy timeline; he understands the recurrence risk and SUDEP information provided. No rescue medication currently prescribed. Pre-conception counselling (paternal): - We discussed heritable risk: for idiopathic epilepsies the absolute risk to offspring is modestly increased compared to background but remains low overall; precise risk depends on the final syndromic classification. Genetic testing is not currently indicated based on history and normal MRI; we will reconsider if further clinical features emerge. - ASM considerations: if medication is initiated, a broad-spectrum agent with favourable teratogenic profile for partners planning pregnancy was discussed. We outlined the need to avoid sodium valproate. He was advised on adherence, sleep optimisation, and minimising alcohol. - Safety: night-time supervision strategies, seizure first aid for partner, and avoidance of high-risk activities (heights, open water, operating heavy machinery) until seizure control is established. DVLA guidance was explained: following nocturnal seizures he must meet regulations for driving; he has currently stopped driving and will follow medical advice and statutory periods. Plan: 1) Provide written information on paternal pre-conception counselling, SUDEP, and seizure first aid. 2) Sleep hygiene and alcohol reduction measures. 3) Arrange sleep-deprived EEG in 6–8 weeks to characterise interictal abnormalities during drowsiness and sleep. 4) If further seizures occur or if he and his partner proceed with pregnancy plans sooner, we will commence a broad-spectrum ASM after shared decision-making; emergency access advice provided. 5) Liaise with primary care for workplace risk assessment support and DVLA notification guidance. 6) Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if breakthrough events occur. He and his partner have contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 14 June 2015 Dr Amelia Patel St George’s Hospital Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Amelia Patel, Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1988, Hospital No: H473920 NHS No. 9938475612 18 Willow Lane, Wimbledon, London SW19 2PA Diagnoses: Two unprovoked seizures under evaluation; EEG pending (booked July 2015). Current Medication: No regular antiepileptic medication at present. PRN buccal midazolam not prescribed. Plan: - Arrange routine EEG and brain MRI with epilepsy protocol. - Provide written seizure first-aid and SUDEP risk counselling. - Discuss driving regulations and notify DVLA as appropriate. - Review in clinic after investigations; earlier if further events occur. - Liaise with community pharmacy regarding continuity of supply if treatment is initiated. I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today following two recent events suggestive of seizures. The first seizure was reported in April 2015 while visiting relatives in Canada. It happened during an afternoon nap, with an unusual tingling spreading from the right hand to the shoulder. The second event took place in June 2015 in the USA, again from sleep, lasting approximately five minutes, with comparable symptoms. There was no clear precipitant identified. There is no personal history of significant head injury, CNS infection, or febrile convulsions. Family history is non-contributory by the patient’s account. Alcohol intake is modest and there is no recreational drug use reported. Sleep had been irregular around the times of travel. Past variability in pharmacy supply is documented in the records from previous long-term prescriptions for non-neurological conditions; the patient reports that adherence was impacted at times when pharmacies substituted brands or experienced stock interruptions. We discussed the importance of consistency of supply should an antiseizure medicine be commenced, and I will ensure any future prescription specifies brand consistency and that the community pharmacy is briefed to minimise switching. On examination today, general and neurological examinations were normal. Observations were stable. There are no lateralising signs. Given the limited number of events, absence of ongoing neurological deficit, and pending investigations, we agreed not to start an antiseizure medication today. Should there be any recurrence, especially with evolving features, we will reconsider treatment promptly. The patient has been advised on sleep hygiene, avoidance of sleep deprivation, and to keep a clear record of any further episodes including timing, duration, semiology, and potential triggers. I have advised that they must not drive and should follow DVLA guidance for a first unprovoked seizure, with notification to the DVLA; I have provided supporting documentation. Workplace safety and water safety precautions were reviewed. A seizure action plan and emergency guidance have been supplied. I will see Michael Turner after the EEG and MRI are completed, or sooner if further events occur. Please let me know if there are questions or if additional information from primary care becomes available. With best wishes,

He reports improved confidence with day-to-day activities and is now walking 30 minutes most days without unsteadiness. Sleep and appetite are stable. rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 09 June 2022 Dr Patel St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Neurology Outpatients, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Michael Harris, DOB: 14-11-1988, Hospital No: NHS-8475021 NHS No. 1075639842 Flat 12, 8 Brookside Way, London, SW9 3LT Diagnoses: Seizure disorder (type not established). He works at a busy metro station gate line where prolonged standing and crowd surges are routine. He attended today with his partner. He reports that heat, dehydration during long shifts, and missed breaks have previously coincided with brief absences and post‑event fatigue. He has been adhering to his current antiseizure medication, and occupational health adjustments (hydration prompts, scheduled micro‑breaks, and access to a staff rest area) were discussed. Following two episodes of dizziness and subsequent headaches, his symptoms improved with supportive care. On 09/May the absences diminished after dose escalation. His last episode was recorded on 17/May and he has remained well since. Considering that he has now been free of seizures for two weeks and his overall condition is stable, no immediate action is necessary. Neurological examination today was unremarkable. No new red‑flag features were elicited. He has a personal seizure action plan at work and carries rescue instructions with supervisor awareness. He is keeping a diary logging shift times, hydration, and any aura‑like sensations; this will be reviewed at follow‑up. Bloods from last month (U&Es, LFTs, FBC) were within normal limits. Pending items: repeat serum drug level prior to next visit to ensure the recent dose change is therapeutic without adverse effects. Plan: - Continue current medication dose and adherence. - Maintain workplace measures (regular hydration and scheduled breaks where feasible). - Seizure diary to continue; bring to next appointment. - Safety advice reiterated regarding operating near moving crowds; avoid lone working during any prodromal symptoms. - Routine follow‑up in three months, sooner if breakthrough events occur. Yours sincerely

The consultation was conducted with the carer’s support and brief use of simplified questions. A communication passport was provided and cross-checked with the home seizure diary. Some characters in prior paperwork appeared garbled (e.g. Ã‚Â·, ï¿½, â€), but the clinical content was clear enough to corroborate the recent history. rows.note_text: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 15 August 2015 Dr Priya Menon University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Priya Menon, Emily Carter, DOB: 22-11-1987, Hospital No: U914735 NHS No. 3849201567 Flat 12, 4 Arundel Yard, London, WC2N 5DR Summary/Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with retained awareness episodes; history of migraine without aura; stage lighting technician with frequent exposure to strobe/bright lights; colleagues may occasionally witness events; mild anxiety symptoms. Medication: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. Propranolol 10 mg as required for performance anxiety. Vitamin D 800 IU daily. No known drug allergies. Thank you for asking me to review this patient in the epilepsy clinic. She works as a stage lighting technician and reports frequent occupational exposure to strobe and very bright moving lights. She and her colleagues have noticed brief spells where she pauses and experiences a rising epigastric sensation with tingling in the right hand and transient difficulty finding words, typically lasting 30–60 seconds without loss of awareness. There is no tongue biting, no incontinence, and recovery is rapid. Epilepsy classification: The semiology and history are in keeping with focal epilepsy. She has no history suggestive of generalised tonic–clonic seizures. There is no known family history of epilepsy. She does not drink to excess and does not use recreational drugs. Sleep can be irregular during show runs. Seizures: She presented with dizziness and headaches on consecutive days, but these resolved spontaneously. On 14/May, following the use of her prescribed medication, the absences became less frequent. The last such episode occurred on 20/May and she has been stable since. Given her stability now, I do not propose further intervention for now. For clarity, the events she describes as “absences” correspond to her brief focal aware episodes. Examination: Neurological examination today was normal. Gait normal. No focal deficits. Investigations: Previous MRI brain (report available) showed no structural lesion. Routine EEG last year demonstrated intermittent left temporal sharp activity without generalised discharges. Occupational context: We discussed strobe exposure and she will continue to use agreed workplace measures (avoiding direct strobe view during programming, scheduled breaks, and ensuring adequate sleep). Colleagues are aware of the brief focal episodes and have been advised on simple first aid and observation. Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. - No dose changes at present given current stability. - Maintain regular sleep and minimise direct strobe exposure where practicable. - Safety advice provided; she does not drive. - Review in 6 months, or sooner if recurrence, change in semiology, or any loss of awareness events. Yours sincerely

llm_only.raw_evidence: With no recurrence for the past months and overall stable epilepsy... We will review him in clinic in six months
llm_only.raw_rationale: The note explicitly states there has been no recurrence of seizures for the past months (specifically since October, leading up to a January clinic date, implying approximately 3-4 months, but the follow-up is in 6 months and the context implies sustained freedom; however, 'past months' is vague. Let's look closer. 'Since then [23 Oct] he has been well. With no recurrence for the past months'. Clinic date is 16 Jan. That is ~2.5 months. The follow up is in 6 months. Background and current status: They work on the gate line at a busy metro station where prolonged standing, variable sleep patterns due to early shifts, and occasional crowd surges are part of the daily environment. No further tonic-clonic seizures have occurred since 12/2020, although two to three single jerks remain, typically noted at the end of long shifts or on waking after reduced sleep. There is no associated loss of awareness with these jerks and no injuries reported. Current medication: 1. Tegretol Retard 600 mg twice daily 2. Keppra 500 mg twice daily Assessment: Overall control of tonic-clonic events is maintained. The residual brief myoclonic jerks are infrequent and appear situational. Mood and cognition are stable on the current regimen. There have been no reported adverse effects beyond mild tiredness after late finishes. Plan: Given the sustained absence of tonic-clonic seizures and the limited impact of occasional single jerks, we will trial a cautious introduction of Lacosamide to optimise control while monitoring tolerability in the context of physically demanding work. Titration schedule for Lacosamide: - Week 1: 25 mg at night - Week 2: 25 mg twice daily - Week 3: 25 mg in the morning and 50 mg at night - Week 4: 50 mg twice daily Then continue 50 mg twice daily for four months until review. No immediate changes to Tegretol Retard or Keppra during the above titration. If Lacosamide is well tolerated and jerks reduce further without impact on alertness at work, we will consider tapering and stopping Keppra at the next clinic visit. The patient has been advised to maintain consistent sleep where possible, keep adequate hydration during shifts, and report any breakthrough events, side effects, or issues with balance or vision promptly. Follow-up: A review appointment has been arranged in four months. With best wishes,

On occasions she is seizure-free for five consecutive days, followed by a day with multiple events, typically several tonic seizures. She describes these as sudden, brief stiffening episodes with loss of awareness and occasional tongue bite but no incontinence. Her partner has witnessed generalised convulsions twice in the past three months, each lasting under two minutes, with a post-ictal phase of fatigue and mild confusion for up to an hour. She is currently taking Sodium Valproate modified-release 750 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. She reports good adherence, confirmed by pharmacy collection records. Adverse effects include mild weight gain (approximately 3 kg over four months) and intermittent tremor of the hands, more noticeable with anxiety or caffeine. No rash, mood lability, or cognitive complaints beyond transient post-ictal fogginess. She is using folic acid 5 mg o.d. as previously advised. There is no current pregnancy and reliable contraception is in place as discussed at prior visits. Past investigations include EEG in March 2024 demonstrating generalised spike–wave discharges and a normal MRI brain (3T) in 2023. There is a positive family history of epilepsy in a maternal aunt. Sleep deprivation, stress, and missed meals are noted precipitants. Alcohol intake is minimal and she denies recreational drugs. She has not driven and understands the DVLA regulations. On examination today she was well, cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable, and neurological examination was normal between events. Weight 72 kg, BP 118/74 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular. Impression: Generalised epilepsy with persistent breakthrough events despite dual therapy, with a fluctuating pattern as above. Given the current stability between clusters and tolerability of medication, we discussed ongoing risk reduction, adherence, and seizure first aid. We also spoke about the option of ambulatory EEG if the clustering pattern changes or increases, and she is agreeable to consider this if needed. She is keen to continue her present regimen for now and to maintain a seizure diary, including potential triggers and catamenial correlations. Plan: - Continue Sodium Valproate MR 750 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. - Maintain folic acid 5 mg o.d. and reliable contraception; we reviewed preconception counselling in the context of generalised epilepsy. - Seizure diary to track frequency, clustering days, sleep patterns, and triggers. - Safety advice reinforced, including bathing/showering precautions and DVLA guidance. - If an increase in cluster days or convulsive events occurs, we will arrange ambulatory EEG and consider adjunctive therapy. - Review in clinic in 3 months, earlier if seizure frequency worsens or adverse effects emerge. Please let me know if you would like any further information. Yours sincerely

Patel Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr A. He works in a manual, safety‑sensitive environment involving heights and machinery, and both he and his employer have noticed episodes at or around workdays that are impacting his attendance and confidence. He describes a stereotyped spell beginning with a brief sense of internal panic and a rising sensation, followed by several minutes during which he becomes unresponsive to questions, vocalises, and rocks in place according to witnesses. There may be clenched jaw and heavy breathing. He is usually confused afterwards for up to 45–60 minutes with headache and fatigue. He may go five days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with 3 - 4 occurring within 24 hours. These clusters tend to occur later in the week, particularly after early shifts or when he has missed sleep. His partner has also witnessed occasional nocturnal episodes of abrupt arousal with gasping and disorientation, after which he has no memory and feels drained the next morning. He has not yet tolerated several medications tried in the past due to mood changes and dizziness, and is currently taking no regular antiseizure therapy. There is no clear precipitant beyond sleep loss and work‑related stress. He denies alcohol misuse. He has had no recent head injury. There is no history to suggest prolonged convulsive activity, and he has not required emergency treatment in the past year. He reports intermittent low mood, largely related to the unpredictability of the events and concerns about job security. There is no current psychotic symptomatology and no safeguarding concerns were raised. On examination today he was alert and oriented, with normal speech and language between episodes. Cranial nerves, limb power, coordination and gait were unremarkable. Cardiovascular and general examination were within normal limits. Given the description and impact on a safety‑critical occupation, further characterisation is required. I have discussed inpatient video‑EEG telemetry to capture typical events and correlate with EEG, alongside MRI brain with an epilepsy protocol if not recently performed. He is agreeable to this plan. In the interim, he and his employer have been advised to continue existing workplace risk assessments and to avoid lone working at height or around moving machinery until we have clearer information from investigations; he understands this and will liaise with occupational health. We also discussed sleep hygiene, regular medication timing for any future treatments, and keeping a seizure diary to document clusters and potential triggers. I will update you following telemetry and imaging, and we can then consider appropriate therapy and rescue strategies for clusters if indicated. Please let me know if there are additional details from the workplace observations that would help inform the diagnostic work‑up. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr A. Rahman The Lime Tree Health Centre 14 Willow Street Bromley Kent BR1 2AB Dear Dr A. Rahman Thomas Green, DOB: 09-02-1991, Hospital No: H927461 NHS No. 7452019863 Flat 3, 12 Millbank Court, Bromley, BR1 4JP Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient describes both generalised tonic–clonic seizures and focal impaired-awareness events), seizure pattern exacerbated by circadian disruption from rotating night shifts MRI brain 2018 reported structurally normal brain; routine EEG 2018 showed intermittent generalised spike–wave with occasional left temporal sharp transients; sleep-deprived EEG 2021 with generalised polyspike–wave and rare left temporal spikes, consistent with combined generalised and focal epileptiform activity Previous medication: Valproate (effective for generalised seizures but stopped due to weight gain and tremor), Carbamazepine (worsened generalised discharges), Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (partial benefit), Clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but sedation), Topiramate (word-finding difficulty), Zonisamide (insomnia), Lacosamide (limited benefit), Perampanel (mood effects) Not taken: Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Rufinamide, Ethosuximide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine Other background: Shift-based employment including nights; longstanding irregular sleep; no history of significant head injury; no family history of epilepsy; does not drive I reviewed Thomas Green in clinic today. He attended alone and provided a detailed diary covering the past three months. He reports that sleep disruption from rotating shifts is a major trigger. He may go four days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with three occurring within 24 hours. Within these clusters he typically experiences brief focal impaired-awareness episodes (staring, automatisms, loss of awareness for 1–2 minutes) sometimes preceded by an epigastric rising sensation, and on some occasions these are followed later the same day by a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. He also describes occasional early-morning generalised seizures after consecutive night shifts. Post-ictally he is fatigued with myalgia and mild confusion for several hours. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily - Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily - Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used approximately twice monthly) Adverse effects: reports irritability on levetiracetam mitigated somewhat with dose timing and exercise; otherwise tolerating regimen. No recent injuries. He remains abstinent from alcohol on working weeks and drinks minimal caffeine. Examination today: Neurological examination normal. Weight stable, BMI 24. No focal deficits. Blood pressure 122/76. Investigations: U&Es, LFTs, FBC from August 2025 normal; Vitamin D borderline low (51 nmol/L). No evidence of hyponatraemia. ECG last year normal sinus rhythm. Discussion/Plan: - We discussed that his pattern and investigations support a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. We reviewed the role of sleep and circadian stability; he is a rotating shift worker including nights and feels the night-to-day swing is the principal precipitant of clusters. - Medication: continue Lamotrigine 150 mg BD. Reduce Levetiracetam to 750 mg BD trial if mood symptoms persist after we implement sleep measures; if seizures worsen, revert to 1 g BD. Consider Brivaracetam as a future alternative if irritability remains problematic. Continue Clobazam 10 mg nocte PRN at onset of cluster for up to 3 nights; he understands the sedation risk. - Rescue/cluster plan: maintain diary; if three or more focal events occur in 24 hours, he will take Clobazam that night and prioritise sleep recovery. He has agreed to call the epilepsy nurse line if clusters persist beyond 48 hours or any injury occurs. - Occupational guidance: provided a written note supporting trial of forward-rotating shifts and at least two consecutive recovery sleep periods after nights; he will discuss with his employer’s occupational health team. We covered safety at work and at home (showers rather than baths, avoid heights/ladders alone, caution with machinery when sleep-deprived). - Driving: not driving currently; we reiterated DVLA regulations and the need to inform DVLA if applicable. - Lifestyle: advised consistent sleep window on off-duty days, morning light exposure after night shifts, and limiting caffeine after midday. Vitamin D supplementation 1000 IU daily suggested given borderline level (over the counter acceptable). - Further investigations: none urgently required. If control remains suboptimal after schedule adjustments, we will discuss ambulatory EEG to better characterise sleep-related triggers and consider Brivaracetam or Cenobamate depending on response and tolerability. Follow-up: Epilepsy nurse telephone follow-up in 6 weeks to review shift adjustments, mood, and cluster frequency; clinic review in 4 months or earlier if clusters increase in frequency or if he has any generalised seizures despite improved sleep strategy. Please do not hesitate to contact me if further information is required. Thank you for your ongoing care. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 Dr Hannah Patel St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Atkinson Morley Wing, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Hannah Patel, Mr Daniel Reeves, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 9034271562 Flat 3, 12 Willow Grove, Mitcham, CR4 2NH Diagnoses: Primary generalised epilepsy with absence seizures EEG (May 2024): Generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy Current Medication: Sodium Valproate 500 mg bd Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use for clusters) Plan: - Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily - Maintain seizure diary capturing work conditions (heat exposure, duration of exertion) - Liaise with Occupational Health regarding heat mitigation and rest breaks outdoors - Routine review in 4 months, earlier if further deterioration or safety concerns I reviewed Mr Daniel Reeves in clinic today. He works in gardening/groundskeeping outdoors, and he reports that heat and prolonged exertion vary seasonally. Over the last three months, he has noticed a clear increase in brief lapses of awareness while working in warmer conditions and during longer tasks. His absence seizures are now occurring on two - three days of the week, whereas previously they were restricted to once every couple of months. Episodes last 5–10 seconds without falls, tongue biting, or incontinence, but he occasionally needs to pause tasks and has twice misplaced tools during a lapse. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures and no myoclonic jerks reported. Sleep is generally adequate; alcohol minimal; no recent intercurrent illness. He remains adherent to Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily. He uses Clobazam 10 mg at night intermittently when he anticipates clusters; he reports mild morning grogginess but no other adverse effects. He has begun recording ambient temperature and workload in his seizure diary, which may help clarify a seasonal/environmental pattern. We discussed practical, non-prescriptive strategies he has tried at work (seeking shade when available, pacing tasks), which he feels help modestly. Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Given that this is primary generalised epilepsy with current absence predominance and a recent increase in frequency, I have recommended continuing his current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for now while we gather more structured diary data and liaise with Occupational Health regarding feasible adjustments to outdoor duties. If the pattern persists despite environmental measures, we will consider dose optimisation or an alternative adjunct at review. He is aware of DVLA guidance and confirms no driving. Yours sincerely,
