rows.note_text: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 29 December 2021 Dr Susan University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Susan, Emily Carter, DOB: 22-07-1988, Hospital No: E748521 NHS No. 1064938275 Flat 12, 4 Kingfisher Court, London, NW1 5QE Summary/ Diagnoses: Generalised epilepsy with recent deterioration in seizure control; probable medication non-adherence secondary to delayed access to rescue medication and refills due to cleanroom/data-hall workplace restrictions; migraine without aura; vitamin D insufficiency; mild GORD; non-smoker; no current alcohol use. Medication: Sodium Valproate (Depakote) 500 mg twice daily. Lamotrigine 150 mg morning and 200 mg evening. Clobazam 10 mg at night (recently increased from 5 mg in October 2021). Midazolam 10 mg buccal solution as rescue, to be used for seizures >5 minutes or clusters. Omeprazole 20 mg once daily. Vitamin D3 1000 IU once daily. Previous antiepileptic therapies: Levetiracetam (stopped due to mood irritability); Topiramate (stopped due to cognitive slowing and paraesthesiae). I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She attended alone. She works in a controlled cleanroom/data-hall environment with strict badge access and tool-down protocols. She reports that retrieval of rescue medication and obtaining on-time refills are often significantly delayed because her medication cannot be brought into the hall and release from station requires supervisor clearance. As a result, she has missed several doses over the last two months and has noticed a clear worsening of seizure control. She describes increased daytime fatigue, post-ictal confusion lasting up to an hour, and new tongue-biting on two occasions. There have been no reported injuries or head strikes, but she has had two near-falls at work. Seizures: She has generalised epilepsy with typical events comprising abrupt loss of awareness with generalised tonic-clonic activity, lateral tongue-bite, and post-ictal confusion. There are also occasional myoclonic jerks in the mornings when sleep-deprived. She kept a brief calendar record for November and December. In Nov she had four seizures during sleep and 3 while awake. In December she had one in sleep and five while awake. These figures represent a significant deterioration compared with earlier in the year when she had gone several months with only rare myoclonic jerks and no convulsions. There is a clear temporal association between missed or delayed doses and seizure occurrence, particularly on late shifts when access to her medication locker is restricted. Examination: Pulse 72 bpm regular, BP 118/72 mmHg. Neurological examination normal between events. No focal deficits. Gait steady. Investigations: Previous MRI brain (2019) normal. Prior routine EEG (2019) showed generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy. No recent bloods available today. Impression: Generalised epilepsy with clinically significant deterioration in seizure control coinciding with workplace-related delays in rescue medication and refill access leading to missed doses. Risk heightened by shift pattern and environmental constraints. Plan: - Epilepsy medication: Increase Clobazam to 10 mg twice daily as interim measure pending review of adherence solutions and monitoring for sedation. Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily and Lamotrigine 150 mg morning/200 mg evening. - Rescue medication: Provide duplicate Midazolam 10 mg buccal packs—one retained with Occupational Health outside the cleanroom and one in a personal grab-bag at the security desk to minimise retrieval delays. - Occupational adjustments: Letter to employer/Occupational Health requesting a reasonable adjustment to allow timed exit for medication dosing and secure storage at access control; designate trained first-aiders for rescue administration. - Safety: Seizure first-aid advice reiterated; avoid lone working on night shifts; consider temporary restriction from high-risk tasks until control improves. - Monitoring: Check U&Es, LFTs, FBC, vitamin D level, and valproate level; lamotrigine level if available. Arrange 24-hour ambulatory EEG if further breakthrough events despite improved access. - Follow-up: Nurse-led phone review in 4 weeks to assess response and adherence; consultant review in 3 months or sooner if seizures cluster or injuries occur. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 13 June 2025 10:20 To: kch-epilepsy@nhs.net Cc: Dr Ravi Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Hannah O’Neill (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Post-partum deterioration and treatment adjustment Hi Emily Epilepsy Diagnosis: Focal epilepsy, probable temporal lobe onset, with secondary generalisation reported on two occasions historically. Patient has focal epilepsy. Present Medication: 1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily 2. Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily Present Seizure Frequency: Since delivery six months ago, the patient reports a perceived worsening of seizures alongside low mood and marked fatigue. In Mar she had five seizures during sleep and 5 while awake. In May she had no in sleep and one while awake. Her partner corroborates that nocturnal events in March included automatisms and post-ictal confusion on waking, while the daytime events were brief focal impaired-awareness episodes with lip smacking and speech arrest, one progressing to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure. Plan of Action: The clinical picture suggests post-partum deterioration, likely influenced by sleep deprivation and mood symptoms. Despite therapeutic lamotrigine levels checked last month, breakthrough focal seizures persist. To address this: - Increase lamotrigine to 200 mg twice daily over two weeks (increase by 25–50 mg per dose every 5–7 days as tolerated), monitoring for rash or dizziness. - Continue levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily unchanged for now. The patient reports irritability and low mood post-partum; we discussed that levetiracetam can exacerbate mood symptoms. If mood remains problematic after lamotrigine optimisation, we will consider tapering levetiracetam and switching to brivaracetam. - Safety: reinforce seizure first aid, no driving as per DVLA guidance following recent events, and avoid unsupervised bathing/co-sleeping with the infant. - Support: referral to perinatal mental health team for assessment of low mood and fatigue; advise sleep hygiene strategies and partner-supported night feeds where possible. - Investigations: arrange repeat EEG with sleep deprivation and an updated MRI epilepsy protocol (last imaging 2019). Check lamotrigine trough level in four weeks after dose escalation. - Follow-up: review in clinic in 8–10 weeks. Earlier review if seizure frequency increases, adverse effects occur, or mood deteriorates further. Overall, the condition is currently deteriorating in the post-partum period by patient and partner report, though May shows partial improvement; we will prioritise seizure control while addressing mood and sleep contributors. With best wishes

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 4 February 2021 Dr A Sharma Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy King’s College Hospital, Denmark Hill, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr A Sharma, Ms Emma Carter, DOB: 22-07-1992, Hospital No: K842917 NHS No. 9384756201 Flat 3, 25 Brook Lane, London, SE15 4AB Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy with nocturnal and occasional daytime events; good response to Sodium Valproate, partial response to Levetiracetam previously; Lamotrigine avoided due to patient-reported mood effects. Other Medical Problems: Post-partum within the last six months; night-time sleep fragmented. Iron deficiency anaemia on oral supplementation. Management Plan: - Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte; maintain single manufacturer brand. - Optimise sleep where possible given infant care; patient to trial shared night feeds three nights per week to reduce sleep fragmentation. - Seizure safety reviewed, including bathing supervision and driving advice (not driving; will reassess per DVLA guidance after seizure-free interval). - Bloods in 8 weeks: valproate level, FBC, LFTs. - Follow-up in three months by video; earlier review if events cluster or daytime seizures increase. History and Current Status: She is six months post-partum and reports substantially broken sleep related to infant care. Against this background, she described the following pattern: In Nov he had 3 seizures during sleep and 1 while awake. In Jan he had five in sleep and one while awake. These events were witnessed by her partner as brief generalised convulsions from sleep with tongue biting and myalgia afterwards; the daytime events were shorter, with transient loss of awareness and brief bilateral shaking. Summary: This patient has generalised epilepsy with recent breakthrough seizures temporally associated with severe sleep disruption in the post-partum period. rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel Riverside Medical Centre 12 Wharf Street, London, SE1 9XX Dear Dr Patel Michael Harris, DOB: 08-05-1987, Hospital No: K839204 NHS No. 7483920012 22 Forge Lane, Flat 3, London, SE8 3QP I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today following ongoing management of generalised epilepsy. He works in metal fabrication and welding, with intermittent exposure to arc light; he reports consistent use of a protective visor and adherence to workplace safety routines. He does not report clear photic-provocation in day-to-day environments, and there have been no definite light-triggered events on site to date. Seizure pattern appears largely unchanged, with events approximately every several days. Occasionally, frequency escalates to daily, and he required midazolam rescue in July and September. He and his partner describe typical generalised tonic–clonic seizures without a focal onset aura, occasionally preceded by brief behavioural arrest and subtle myoclonic jerks in the early morning. There is post-ictal confusion and fatigue lasting several hours. No injuries since the last review, and no episodes at the workplace in the past month. Sleep disruption and missed evening doses have coincided with the periods of clustering. He is currently taking Sodium Valproate 1 g b.d., Levetiracetam 1.5 g b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He reports satisfactory tolerability overall, with mild daytime somnolence and intermittent low mood but no rash, diplopia, or gastrointestinal upset. Weight stable. He rarely uses buccal midazolam as a rescue medication per prior plan, administered by his partner when clusters emerge. We discussed generalised epilepsy self-management and the importance of sleep regularity and strict medication adherence. He confirms that his employer accommodates regular breaks and that he uses a full-face auto-darkening visor and gloves for welding tasks; he also avoids working alone. He has informed occupational health of his diagnosis. He does not drive. I have requested an updated EEG with photic stimulation given his occupational exposure, and routine bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) to monitor therapy. He prefers not to adjust medication today; given tolerability and the overall stability outside the brief clusters, I agreed to continue current doses pending the EEG and blood results. We also reviewed the rescue plan and thresholds for seeking urgent care. I will see him again in three months, or earlier if there is an increase in seizure-related injury, change in semiology, or further need for rescue therapy. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 17 September 2025 Dr Jonathan Hale Maple Grove Health Centre 12 Maple Grove, Bromley Kent BR2 8QP Dear Dr Jonathan Hale Re: Wendy Brown, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: K482715 NHS No. 6592841037 Flat 7 Brookside Avenue, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 2QD Diagnoses/summary: Longstanding seizure disorder with prior normal structural imaging (MRI 2006 reported no epileptogenic lesion). Multiple prior anti-seizure medication trials with limited benefit and tolerability issues. Social stressors and increased alcohol exposure recently. Ã‚Â· Current concerns: I reviewed Wendy Brown in clinic today, accompanied by a close friend. Over the past 3–4 months she reports escalating social pressures related to job insecurity and family matters, with higher alcohol exposure at social events, despite attempts to moderate intake. She feels more fatigued, with reduced concentration and disrupted sleep. She describes a change in her day-to-day functioning: increased time off work, heightened anxiety, and lower confidence when going out alone. She and her partner had been exploring future family options but have placed this on hold given the recent deterioration. ï¿½ Seizure history and current pattern: Seizures are occurring with a clustering pattern, most often every 5 days, with occasional short periods of increased frequency. Rescue medication has been needed on 1 occasions this year. No clear progression compared to previous follow-up. Despite the wording above, from a holistic standpoint her overall wellbeing and social impact have worsened, and she finds post-event recovery slower with more prominent cognitive fog and headaches. Family witnesses describe brief behavioural arrest with non-responsiveness and occasional confusion afterwards, sometimes preceded by nausea and a sense of dread. There is no consistent trigger identified, though poor sleep and alcohol intake appear temporally associated. â€ Investigations: Prior telemetries/EEGs performed on more than one occasion; no definitive lesion on MRI (2006). No new imaging since last review. We discussed repeat imaging and prolonged EEG if symptoms continue to affect function. Ã© Medication history: - Previously tried: Levetiracetam (seizures persisted, noted irritability and fatigue), Clobazam (regular and PRN), Gabapentin, Carbamazepine, Phenobarbital, Phenytoin, Valproate, Vigabatrin, Lacosamide (ceased due to side-effects and limited efficacy). - Not taken to date: Pregabalin, Topiramate, Zonisamide, Tiagabine, Acetazolamide, Primidone, Perampanel, Retigabine, Rufinamide. Current regular medicines reported today: - Lamotrigine 150 mg morning, 100 mg midday, 100 mg evening (dose increased previously by 50 mg without clear benefit) - Metoclopramide PRN for nausea - Folic acid 5 mg daily and a general vitamin/mineral supplement Adverse effects/risks: She reports intermittent headaches, gastric discomfort under investigation by her GP (possible biliary colic, previously small gallstone query), and marked tiredness. No new focal neurological deficits reported. She denies visual blurring suggestive of acute ocular issues. Psychosocial context and deterioration: The patient feels her condition is deteriorating in practical and psychosocial terms: more time off work, reduced independence, and increased reliance on family support. She links recent slippage in routine (late nights, increased alcohol in social settings) to worse symptom control, despite efforts to cut back. We discussed sleep hygiene, alcohol minimisation, and stress management strategies, which she is motivated to pursue. ï¿½ Management discussion today: - We reviewed non-pharmacological measures including structured sleep routine, alcohol avoidance, and stress reduction approaches. She will continue a seizure diary noting sleep, alcohol, and stress exposures. - We revisited device therapies discussed historically (including VNS), and she remains open to reconsidering if day-to-day impact remains high. - We discussed medication options she has not yet tried. Given recent functional deterioration and ongoing events, she wishes to consider a cautious trial of Topiramate with slow uptitration if tolerated, acknowledging potential side-effects (weight loss, cognitive slowing, mood change, paraesthesia, and rare ocular complications). She has been advised on adequate hydration. Plan: 1) Initiate Topiramate 25 mg nocte for 2 weeks, then increase by 25 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated, aiming initially for 50 mg twice daily. If adverse effects occur, hold or reduce to last tolerated dose. â€ 2) Continue Lamotrigine at current doses for now; potential rationalisation to be reviewed based on response and tolerability. 3) Arrange nurse-led telephone reviews every 4–6 weeks to monitor side-effects, adherence, and seizure diary trends. 4) Provide written advice on alcohol minimisation, sleep regularity, and safety measures. Rescue plan reinforced. 5) Consider repeat MRI with epilepsy protocol and prolonged EEG if functional impact persists at next review. 6) Routine follow-up in 4 months, with earlier appointment if deterioration continues or adverse effects emerge. Thank you for your support with the above. Please feel free to contact me if there are any concerns or if earlier review would be helpful. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Ahmed St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Ahmed, Thomas Reid, DOB: 12-04-1986, Hospital No: R518203 NHS No. 9843216750 23 Gardeners Row, London, W10 5PL Medication: Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. Clobazam 10 mg at night as needed for clusters. Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS) active; patient-initiated magnet use. Rescue: Buccolam 10 mg buccal as directed for prolonged clusters. I reviewed Thomas Reid in clinic today. He works outdoors in gardening and groundskeeping, noting that heat and prolonged exertion vary by season and can make him feel more fatigued on summer afternoons. He has been careful with hydration and pacing, and he takes brief shade breaks when feasible. He does not drive. His seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced four days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 4 months. He reports that clusters are more likely after consecutive long days in hot weather; during cooler weeks he experiences fewer daytime events and relies less on the VNS magnet. Night-time rest has improved since adopting earlier bedtimes on work nights. There have been no injuries, and postictal recovery is usually under an hour. He feels Levetiracetam is well tolerated without mood change. Clobazam is kept for early cluster signs, especially when he anticipates multiple consecutive outdoor shifts. He has a clear rescue plan at work: a colleague is aware of Buccolam location and when to contact emergency services. No missed doses reported. We discussed practical measures he is already using at work—regular fluid intake, lighter tasks during peak heat when possible, and scheduled breaks. He will continue to record seizure timing relative to shift length, ambient temperature, and hydration, which may help us refine strategies. He will also note magnet use and any Buccolam doses. Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable; no concerns raised regarding skin integrity or dehydration. VNS site looks healthy with no local tenderness. Plan: - Continue Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. - Continue access to Clobazam 10 mg at night for clusters as currently used. - Maintain VNS magnet strategy and workplace rescue protocol with Buccolam available. - Keep detailed seizure and trigger diary including work conditions (heat/exertion), hydration, and sleep. - We will review in four months or sooner if seizure clusters escalate or rescue medication is required more than monthly. We will see him back in four months. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 February 2019 Dr Amelia Reid Riverside Medical Centre 12 Wharf Street, London, SE8 3AB Dear Dr Amelia Reid Michael Turner, DOB: 14-02-1991, Hospital No: H829374 NHS No. 7465129380 22A Lockside Mews, London, SE8 4PL Thank you for referring the above patient back to the Neurology Clinic. I reviewed him today following the birth of his child within the last six months. He reports that night-time sleep has been fragmented since the baby arrived, with multiple awakenings most nights. He has a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy; he and his partner describe events consistent with both generalised convulsive seizures and focal impaired awareness episodes. He identifies occasional focal auras (brief rising epigastric sensation and sudden pause in activity) that sometimes progress, and there have been intermittent generalised tonic–clonic seizures, often out of sleep. Regarding current seizure pattern, his seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced four to five days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 4 months. He reports that cluster occurrence appears worse after several consecutive nights of disrupted sleep. His partner keeps a diary that broadly corroborates this pattern. Current treatment includes Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte with an additional 5–10 mg as needed for clusters on clinician advice in the past. He has an implanted Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS) which he swipes more often during prodromal symptoms, particularly overnight. Rescue medication is Buccolam (midazolam) oromucosal, which he has required approximately once per month over the last four months, with good effect and no reported adverse reactions other than transient drowsiness. He denies new rashes, visual disturbance, or ataxia. He notes increased daytime fatigue, which he attributes to poor sleep and cumulative medication effects. Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological examination was non-focal. Observations were stable. No tongue lacerations or injuries reported since the last visit. We discussed the likely contribution of sleep fragmentation to seizure clustering. He remains motivated to continue VNS use and maintain a seizure diary. He has not driven. We reviewed SUDEP awareness and general safety measures, particularly around infant care and night-time supervision. He and his partner have put in place practical strategies (monitoring and alternating night duties) and feel these are helping. Plan: - Continue Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte with previously advised as-needed dosing for clusters. - Continue VNS with magnet use at aura or early cluster onset as currently practised. - Maintain seizure and sleep diary to document cluster timing relative to sleep disruption. - Reinforce rescue protocol with Buccolam as previously instructed; partner is confident in administration. - Arrange ambulatory EEG to sample nocturnal periods given concern for sleep-related exacerbation. - Refer to epilepsy specialist nurse for counselling on sleep hygiene and practical seizure management in the post-partum context. - Safety advice reiterated; he is not driving and will continue to adhere to DVLA guidance. I will review him in three months or sooner if clusters escalate or rescue medication is required more frequently than current use. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Emily Carter, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H473920 NHS No. 9384756201 Flat 12, 28 Wandsworth Road, London, SW8 2LG Diagnoses: Recurrent epileptic seizures of uncertain classification; possible catamenial association based on patient-reported menstrual tracking app entries. Current Medication: - Levetiracetam 1 g bd - Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use per seizure clusters) - Buccolam (midazolam) oromucosal 10 mg for prolonged seizures as per rescue protocol - Vagus Nerve Stimulator in situ (implanted 2023) Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure regimen unchanged at present. - Maintain detailed seizure and menstrual cycle tracking; patient to continue using menstrual tracking app and share exports before next review. - Rescue plan reaffirmed: Buccolam for prolonged events, with clear guidance to seek urgent care if clusters persist beyond usual pattern. - Consider perimenstrual clobazam “pulsed” strategy if pattern persists; to be reviewed at next appointment once further correlation is confirmed. - Check serum levetiracetam level, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, vitamin D. - VNS settings to be reviewed in device clinic; encourage on-demand magnet use as trained. - Safety advice reinforced including SUDEP risk minimisation, adherence, and avoiding known personal triggers where possible. - Follow up in 4 months, sooner if deterioration. I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She reports a variable pattern of seizures over recent months, and has been keeping a detailed diary alongside a menstrual tracking app. The entries suggest clustering around specific cycle phases, and she will continue to track this to help clarify any catamenial association. His seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced 5 days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 3 months. There have been no injuries, and recovery has been quicker when on-demand VNS is applied promptly. She feels that sleep disruption and acute stress may contribute, and has started consistent sleep and hydration routines. She is tolerating levetiracetam without mood change, and uses clobazam intermittently during anticipated clusters. Previously his focal seizures were rare, brief, and stereotyped with right-hand tingling and preserved awareness. Since late summer he has noticed nocturnal events, occasional head deviation, and post-event confusion lasting 20–40 minutes, which is a new event phenotype when compared with his baseline pattern. He also reports new morning myalgia and tongue soreness on two occasions. There have been no clear triggers identified, though sleep fragmentation and recent work stress were noted. Seizures: He had a cluster of three seizures in Aug (short, not full convulsions, fluctuating awareness, self-terminating). Motor: full power throughout, no pronator drift. Sensation grossly intact. Coordination normal. Gait narrow-based but steady. No focal neurological deficit identified today. Investigations to date: Last lamotrigine and levetiracetam levels checked March 2023 (within reference). MRI brain (2021) demonstrated left frontal gliosis without progression; routine EEG (2020) showed left frontotemporal sharp waves. No recent bloods available from primary care. Assessment: Focal epilepsy with a clinically significant deterioration and emergence of a new event phenotype suggestive of evolving focal to bilateral risk. The pattern of nocturnal events and a documented tonic seizure at respite signify increased seizure burden compared with his prior course. Plan: - Safety: Reinforced SUDEP and safety counselling; advised strict nocturnal supervision measures and seizure alarm use as discussed. Driving: not driving and remains unfit to drive; DVLA guidance reiterated. - Medication: Continue levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily pending levels. We will consider lamotrigine uptitration versus adjunct lacosamide after results and EEG review. - Tests: Request urgent anti-seizure medication trough levels, U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D. Arrange sleep-deprived EEG and ambulatory EEG to capture nocturnal events. Partner to continue detailed event diary and, where feasible, obtain brief video during events. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 9 May 2017 Dr Ahmed St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Ahmed, Mateo Alvarez, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: H938271 NHS No. 5839201746 12 Brookfield Road, London, W10 5RA Medication: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, commenced following initial assessment in primary care after recent events. Patient reports good adherence, with occasional missed morning doses during shift work. No notable adverse effects beyond mild irritability in the first fortnight, now settled. History and interval events: Mateo Alvarez is a recent migrant to the UK and is still learning how to navigate NHS services; he has occasionally attended with interpreter support. He has received our written safety advice translated into his preferred language and confirms understanding. Since initial review by the GP, the pattern of episodes has been clarified as follows: In November he presented with a cluster of three seizures (self-terminating, fluctuating awareness). In February a nocturnal seizure were noted, and in April a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure occurred (not witnessed by family). No clear precipitants identified; he reports variable sleep due to new employment and some stress around housing paperwork. There is no history of significant head injury, CNS infection, or family history of similar episodes. Examination today is unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory and neurological findings. He is oriented, with no focal deficits. Investigations: - Baseline bloods in primary care reported as within reference ranges (U&E, LFT, FBC). - We have arranged a routine EEG and MRI brain with epilepsy protocol; appointments have been requested with attention to interpreter availability. - DVLA guidance and safety precautions (bathing/swimming supervision, heights, machinery) discussed and provided in writing; he confirms he will refrain from driving and has initiated self-notification. Plan: 1) Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for now; we will review dosing after EEG/MRI and in light of any further events. 2) Seizure diary provided; he will record sleep patterns, missed doses, and any alcohol intake to help identify triggers. 3) Written first aid guidance shared with family; he has consented to us sending a summary to his workplace occupational health. 4) Interpreter-supported follow-up booked for 12 weeks, sooner if further seizures occur or adverse effects develop. 5) Signposted to local community support and an information session on accessing NHS appointments, including how to request interpreters in advance. We will update you when investigations are available. Please contact us if there are interim concerns or if further events occur. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 23 August 2010 Dr Sarah Ahmed Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy St. Bartholomew’s Hospital, London Dear Dr Sarah Ahmed, Emma Carter, DOB: 12-06-1996, Hospital No: A837462 NHS No. 2045891173 Flat 3, 22 Brook Lane, London, SE5 9QH Diagnosis: Focal epilepsy with good response to Lamotrigine; Levetiracetam previously ineffective; Phenytoin not tolerated due to dizziness and cognitive slowing. Aetiology: Perinatal infarct affecting the right parietal region (radiologically stable on prior imaging). Other Medical Problems: Vitamin D insufficiency on supplementation; mild migraine without aura; no known drug allergies. Background and Recent Events: She wears a smartwatch with fall-detection enabled; the device logs have been useful in corroborating the timing of events when available. In Mar she experienced a prolonged focal seizure lasting 8 minutes, resolving without intervention. In May there were three further brief absences, and in Aug a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure was reported at school (not witnessed by family). The school nurse documented a post-ictal phase of approximately 15 minutes; the smartwatch registered a hard fall alert at the corresponding time. There have been no emergency department attendances, and there has been no reported injury. Current Treatment: Lamotrigine 150 mg mane and 200 mg nocte, single brand only. Buccal midazolam rescue pack held at school and home but not administered during the above events. Management Plan: - Continue Lamotrigine at current dosing and maintain single-brand supply to avoid variability. - Arrange serum Lamotrigine level and vitamin D recheck prior to next review. - School has been provided with updated seizure first-aid guidance; smartwatch fall alerts to be printed from the companion app to support event chronology. - No driving. Occupational advice provided regarding graded return to PE participation at school with supervision. Summary: This patient has focal epilepsy attributed to a perinatal parietal infarct. Event chronology over the past six months is as above, with smartwatch data aiding correlation of timings. No medication changes are proposed today given overall tolerability and absence of clustering or status features. I will review in six months or sooner if further generalised events occur. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 14 June 2020 Dr Kate Health Centre Keele University, Keele, Newcastle Staffordshire ST5 5BG Dear Dr Kate Amelia Jones, DOB: 12-03-1994, Hospital No: K593021 NHS No. 7483926150 12 Orchard Mews, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 1AB Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with history of childhood febrile seizures; current clinical focus is adult epilepsy management. No known structural brain abnormality on prior imaging (patient-reported MRI in 2017 normal). Family history negative for epilepsy. No learning disability. No known cardiac history. Previous medication: Sodium valproate (discontinued due to weight gain and tremor), levetiracetam (mood irritability), clonazepam PRN for clusters, ethosuximide in childhood (for absences). Not taken/trialled to date: lamotrigine, topiramate, zonisamide, perampanel, brivaracetam, lacosamide, cannabidiol. Allergies: No known drug allergies. I reviewed Amelia Jones in clinic today, accompanied by her partner. She reports a longstanding history of generalised epilepsy with onset in late adolescence, against a background of childhood febrile seizures. She has had variable control over the last year and is keeping a seizure diary. Seizure history since last review: A prolonged event occurred in December (approximately 12 minutes, alternating between focal and generalised features, settled spontaneously). In March she had a drop attack, and in May five myoclonic jerks were documented at college (not observed directly by parents). She denies intercurrent illness or missed doses around these events. No injuries apart from minor bruising with the March episode. She reports early morning myoclonus about once weekly otherwise, and occasional brief absences per her description (brief staring with rapid recovery), though not all have been witnessed. Current medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily (self-reduced to 750 mg in the morning for two weeks due to irritability, now back to 1000 mg BD), folic acid 400 micrograms daily, vitamin D 1000 IU daily. No contraception interactions anticipated; she uses a copper IUD. She does not drive. Examination: General and neurological examination today was normal. Weight stable; BMI 23.4. No focal deficits. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Investigations: Routine EEG in 2019 reportedly showed generalised spike-and-wave bursts with photoparoxysmal response (report seen). No recent bloods; we will check U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, and TSH. Discussion: We discussed that her pattern is consistent with generalised epilepsy, with variable myoclonus and probable absences; the December event suggests secondary generalisation or a longer generalised tonic–clonic seizure with fluctuating semiology as per witness account. Mood side effects on levetiracetam remain a concern. We reviewed treatment options including switching to or adding lamotrigine or topiramate, and non-pharmacological measures (sleep regularity, alcohol avoidance, adherence). We also discussed SUDEP risk reduction strategies and seizure first aid with her partner. Plan: - Transition plan to lamotrigine: initiate 25 mg once daily for 2 weeks, then 25 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then 50 mg twice daily, aiming for 100 mg twice daily as tolerated. We will then consider tapering levetiracetam depending on response. - Provide written titration schedule and adverse effect counselling (rash/Stevens–Johnson, dizziness, ataxia). She understands to seek urgent advice if rash develops. - Rescue plan: clonazepam 0.5 mg orally for clusters of myoclonus or prolonged absence sequences, maximum 1 mg in 24 hours; partner instructed regarding when to call 999 (convulsive seizure >5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, injury). - Blood tests today: FBC, U&E, LFT, TSH, vitamin D. - Safety: reinforced avoidance of swimming alone, heights, and open flames; continue not driving in line with DVLA guidance. - Follow-up: nurse specialist telephone review in 4 weeks to assess tolerability and diary; clinic review in 3 months, sooner if deterioration. Thank you for your ongoing care and for prescribing lamotrigine per the above titration if local protocol permits. Please let me know if there are any concerns. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 11 February 2016 Dr Amelia Green St Helier Neurology Clinic Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals, Neurology Department, Wrythe Lane, Carshalton SM5 1AA Dear Dr Amelia Green, Emily Carter, DOB: 14-03-2001, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 6031847295 29 Meadowbank Close, Sutton, SM2 6QL Diagnoses: Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification; prior EEG non-diagnostic. Current Medication: Lamotrigine 75 mg bd Plan: Continue current antiepileptic therapy; reinforce seizure first-aid education; maintain seizure diary; routine follow-up in 12 months or earlier if further events occur. I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She attended with her mother, who provided additional collateral history. She has previously practised aura recognition strategies with our epilepsy nurse team and continues to describe warning features in her own words as a "hollow, rising feeling in the chest with a brief sense of detachment" lasting 10–20 seconds, typically occurring before more obvious events. Over the last several months there has been a variable pattern of episodes: In August she experienced a prolonged focal seizure lasting 8 minutes, resolving without intervention. In October there were two further brief absences, and in January a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure was reported at school (not witnessed by family). She reports good adherence to Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily and denies missed doses. She and her mother have kept a diary noting sleep disruption as a possible trigger. There is no recent intercurrent illness, alcohol exposure, or new medications. Neurological examination in clinic today was normal. There is no injury history from the January event, and recovery was described as gradual but complete within several hours. There is no consistent diurnal pattern reported. We discussed ongoing management. She finds the aura recognition techniques helpful to prompt sitting down, alerting staff, and ensuring a safe environment. She understands standard seizure first-aid and the school has a care plan. We agreed to continue Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily without dose change for now, as tolerability remains good and there are no reported adverse effects (no rash, mood change, or dizziness). I have asked her to maintain a detailed diary, including aura descriptions, potential triggers, and any witness reports from school. We will also request updated school incident documentation to clarify semiology where available. I have arranged routine follow-up in 12 months, with open access to earlier review if there are further prolonged events, clusters, or any injuries. She was given advice on sleep hygiene and safety, including supervision around water and avoidance of heights when a warning is present. With best wishes,

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 3 October 2015 Dr Anita Shah Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy Kingston Hospital NHS Foundation Trust Dear Dr Anita Shah, Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-08-1992, Hospital No: K847210 NHS No. 3014729986 Flat 12, 9 Riverbank Way, Kingston upon Thames, KT1 2AB Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy with recent clusters of brief seizures; valproate responsive but with residual breakthrough episodes Aetiology: Presumed genetic generalised epilepsy; no structural lesion identified; normal development and no perinatal complications Other Medical Problems: Generalised anxiety and low mood, patient reports intermittent sleep disturbance and health-related worry; no self-harm; currently engaged with GP for talking therapy referral Management Plan: - Continue sodium valproate modified release 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte. - Introduce rescue plan for clusters: buccal midazolam 5 mg if three or more brief seizures occur within 30 minutes, or if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes; mother instructed and provided written guidance. - Sleep hygiene advice and stress-management strategies discussed; encourage ongoing counselling via IAPT. - Safety advice: avoid sleep deprivation, limit alcohol, and adhere to DVLA guidance for seizures. - Arrange ambulatory EEG and serum valproate level prior to next visit; routine bloods including FBC, LFTs. - Review in four months, earlier if further clusters occur. rows.note_text: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 15 May 2011 Dr Amelia Grant St. Bartholomew’s Hospital Department of Neurology, West Smithfield, London EC1A 7BE Dear Dr Amelia Grant, Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1976, Hospital No: H392744 NHS No. 9045127763 Flat 2, 18 Brookside Lane, Enfield, London EN2 7QX Diagnoses: Recurrent seizures of unclear classification; prior normal neuroimaging (2010); no clear precipitant identified. Current Medication: Levetiracetam 500 mg bd Clobazam 5 mg nocte prn for clusters Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. - Safety advice reinforced for outdoor manual work in heat and during prolonged exertion; patient to take regular shaded breaks and maintain hydration. - Driving advice per DVLA guidance discussed and understood. - Arrange repeat EEG and ambulatory ECG to explore reported drop attacks. - Follow up in 4 months, or sooner if further events occur. I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He works in gardening and groundskeeping outdoors, where heat exposure and prolonged exertion vary seasonally. He reports that fluctuations in temperature and workload can affect his fatigue levels. Since his last appointment in November, he has kept a detailed diary of events. In Dec 3 brief absences were reported. In Mar 5 drop attacks occurred, and in Apr another tonic seizure was recorded. The absences were described as sudden pauses with unresponsiveness lasting a few seconds, without clear warning, followed by rapid recovery. The drop attacks were brief with loss of postural tone and immediate reorientation; no clear vertigo, palpitations, or prolonged confusion was noted. The tonic event in April occurred late afternoon after a long shift in warm conditions, with muscle stiffening, a fall, and tongue bite; recovery to baseline took around 30 minutes according to a colleague. There have been no head injuries requiring hospital attendance. He denies alcohol excess and has been sleeping 7–8 hours on most nights, though notes early starts during spring workload peaks. He has not identified consistent auras. Medication adherence has been good; no missed doses reported. There are no new neurological symptoms between events. Routine bloods in March (U&E, LFTs, FBC) were within reference ranges. Prior MRI brain (March 2010) was unremarkable. Given the variety of event types and the occupational context, I have advised ongoing adherence to current treatment, attention to hydration, rest breaks, and avoidance of lone work at height or near machinery when fatigued. We discussed escalation options if further events occur before review, and he will contact the service if frequency increases or injuries occur. An EEG has been requested to characterise the brief absences, and ambulatory ECG arranged to exclude arrhythmic causes for the drop attacks. With best wishes,

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 8 April 2013 Dr Patel North London Neurosciences Centre Neurology Department, 14 Highgate Hill, London N19 5LW Dear Dr Patel, Michael Harris, DOB: 28-02-1981, Hospital No: K593024 NHS No. 7482103659 3A Wren Court, Holloway Road, London N7 6RT Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy, likely frontal onset, with nocturnal predominance. I reviewed Michael Harris in our epilepsy clinic today by scheduled telephone appointment, which he prefers given his frequent international business travel and irregular sleep across time zones. He reports generally good adherence to lamotrigine, with occasional delayed evening doses when flying long-haul. He has been using a mobile app to track time zone changes and dosing times, which appears to have reduced missed doses. He denies adverse effects beyond occasional transient dizziness when sleep-deprived. There is no current use of rescue medication and he has not required emergency services since last year. Seizure history since the last review: In November he had a run of one seizure within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In December there was 7 further seizures at night, and in March another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He associates the November and December events with multiple red-eye flights, jet lag and fragmented sleep. The March episode followed a strenuous rehabilitation session for a minor ankle injury while he was mildly sleep-deprived; there was no reported trauma, tongue biting or incontinence. Post-ictal confusion, when present, is brief. He continues to describe a reliable focal aware aura of a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness; secondary generalisation has not been reported during this interval. Examination is not applicable today as this was a telephone consultation. Review of prior investigations: MRI brain (last year) was structurally normal; routine EEG showed intermittent right frontal sharp activity with increased expression during drowsiness. No changes to his cardiac or metabolic profiles have been noted by his GP in recent blood tests. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. We discussed setting dual time-zone alarms to anchor dosing to home time for flights exceeding 6 hours, shifting by 1–2 hours per day to avoid large dosing gaps. - Provide a written travel seizure plan for airlines and hotel staff; patient to carry a copy on all trips. - Sleep hygiene advice emphasised, particularly avoidance of red-eye flights where feasible and limiting overnight work before major time zone changes. - No rescue medication indicated at present given self-limited events and absence of generalised tonic–clonic seizures; we will revisit if frequency increases. - Arrange ambulatory EEG if nocturnal frequency persists over the next quarter. - Follow-up in three months by telephone, or earlier if there is escalation, injury, or emergence of generalised tonic–clonic seizures. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 25 December 2019 Dr Alicia Nguyen Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Alicia Nguyen Consultant Neurologist, Sophie Patel, DOB: 14-03-1998, Hospital No: K742119 NHS No. 9075634218 12 Grove Park Road, London, SE5 8QL Thank you for asking me to review this patient, who attended with her mother. She is a rotating shift worker, including nights, and both she and her family report marked disruption of her circadian rhythm with variable sleep duration and frequent early morning tiredness on the weeks following night shifts. She describes intermittent brief episodes of disconnection at work and occasional startle-like twitches when overtired. There is no consistent alcohol excess. Caffeine intake fluctuates with shifts. With regard to recent paroxysmal events, the family and patient provided a clear timeline for 2019: A prolonged event occurred in Jul (approximately 12 minutes, alternating between focal and generalised features, settled spontaneously). In Oct she had 5 drop attacks, and in Dec two myoclonic jerks were documented at college (not observed directly by parents). No injuries were sustained. She reports variable post-event fatigue but no prolonged confusion. No consistent aura is recalled. There have been no witnessed nocturnal events at home, although she often wakes unrefreshed after consecutive night duties. Past history is unremarkable for febrile seizures, meningitis, or significant head injury. There is no known family history of seizures. She does not drive. Current medications include only a combined oral contraceptive; she is not taking any antiseizure medication. She denies recreational drug use. Mood is described as generally stable, though she notes irritability when sleep deprived. Appetite is normal. Neurological review of systems otherwise negative. On examination today she was alert and cooperative, oriented, with fluent speech. Cranial nerves intact. Motor, sensory, coordination and gait examinations were normal. No stigmata of systemic disease observed. At present it remains difficult to ascribe a single unifying diagnosis for these events. The reported variability in semiology, the temporal clustering around periods of sleep disruption, and the lack of consistent focal neurologic signs today mean that further objective data are required. I have discussed non-prescriptive strategies she may consider to stabilise her sleep–wake schedule within the constraints of her rota, and she will keep a detailed event and sleep diary, cross-referencing shift pattern, caffeine intake, and any intercurrent illness. She and her mother are comfortable to proceed with further investigations. Plan agreed today (patient-reported preferences included): - Ambulatory EEG with extended montage to sample across a full shift cycle, aiming to capture events on late and night duties. - MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to screen for a structural correlate. - Basic bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid profile, vitamin D, and ferritin. - Request contemporaneous reports from college and workplace first aid/incident logs relating to the Dec jerks and Oct drops, and any CCTV where available, to improve event characterisation. - Safety advice regarding bathing and working at heights has been discussed in clinic terms today; she will review workplace risk assessments with her manager and occupational health. She is aware of DVLA guidance relevance should events continue. I will review her in clinic once the above investigations are completed, or sooner if the frequency or severity of events escalates. She and her mother have our contact details for interim concerns. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 23 March 2026 Dr James Cole Riverside Health Centre 12 Avon Street, Southwark, London SE1 6TU Dear Dr James Cole Daniel Moore, DOB: 17-08-1994, Hospital No: H728391 NHS No. 7712039846 Flat 4, 29 Larkspur Court, London SE15 3QN Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with photosensitivity; stage lighting technician with frequent exposure to strobe/bright lights; colleagues may occasionally witness events. Prior EEG reports (patient-reported) suggest generalised spike–wave discharges consistent with idiopathic generalised epilepsy. No known structural lesion. Previous medication: Sodium valproate (effective but stopped previously due to weight gain and tremor), levetiracetam (mood irritability), lamotrigine (partial benefit), clobazam PRN for clusters (sedation), perampanel (dizziness, behavioural change), topiramate (word-finding difficulty), zonisamide (appetite suppression, low mood). Not taken: brivaracetam, lacosamide, ethosuximide (not trialled as absence prominence uncertain), cannabidiol, rufinamide. Comorbidities/other: Migraine without aura; mild asthma on PRN salbutamol. No known cardiac disease. No learning difficulties. Occupation: stage lighting technician; frequent exposure to high-intensity strobes and LED effects; uses protective strategies at work (breaks, dark adaptation, avoiding direct gaze into fixtures) per supervisor policy. I reviewed Daniel Moore in clinic today. He attended alone. He reports variable daytime alertness, particularly after late finishes at venues, and occasional missed meals when on tour. He notes that colleagues sometimes observe brief staring with eyelid flutter and loss of track of conversation during programming sessions with bright scenes. He keeps a diary and uses a smartwatch, which occasionally flags elevated heart rate preceding events. Sleep is typically 5–6 hours on show days. Seizure history and recent pattern: He has generalised epilepsy, with probable photosensitive component. In December he had a run of 4 seizures within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In February there was 4 further seizures at night, and in March another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He denies tongue biting or significant injury this year; one scalp bump in December eased with rest and ice. No emergency department attendances. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily - Clobazam 10 mg at night (additional 10 mg PRN for clusters, used twice since January) - Folic acid 5 mg daily (patient preference) - Salbutamol inhaler PRN Allergies: No known drug allergies. Examination today: Alert and oriented. Speech fluent. Cranial nerves normal. No focal neurological deficit. Gait normal. Weight stable. No tremor. Investigations: Patient reports prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike–wave and photoparoxysmal response at certain flash frequencies; we have requested the formal reports. No recent MRI; not routinely indicated in idiopathic generalised epilepsy, but patient is happy to forgo unless new focal features emerge. Occupational considerations: We discussed photosensitivity management at work including minimising direct line-of-sight to strobe arrays, using brimmed cap/blue-blocking lenses if helpful, planned breaks, hydration, and sleep hygiene around show days. Colleagues are aware of basic seizure first aid and will maintain a brief witness account when possible. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily. - Trial brivaracetam add-on 50 mg twice daily for two weeks, then 100 mg twice daily if tolerated; advise to stop and contact clinic if marked mood change or dizziness. - Reserve clobazam 10 mg as cluster rescue as currently used; avoid routine daytime dosing given sedation at work. - Arrange EEG with photic stimulation at our centre to characterise photoparoxysmal response and guide workplace adjustments; provide written summary for employer if patient consents. - Provide seizure diary template; encourage smartwatch event tagging to correlate with triggers (strobe sequences, sleep loss, dehydration). - Safety: avoid working at height alone; ensure spotters present during rigging; maintain hydration; prioritise regular meals; discuss driving status separately according to DVLA regulations if applicable to his licence category. - Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if clusters increase or if brivaracetam not tolerated. Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are any concerns or if shared monitoring is needed in the interim. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Centre for Neurology Services Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 9 July 2019 Dr Priya Shah Consultant Neurologist Riverside Neurology Clinic 12 Brook Lane, Manchester M20 5HT Dear Dr Priya Shah, Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-09-1987, Hospital No: M843219 NHS No. 6049927713 Flat 3, 27 Willow Court, Manchester M14 2AB Summary and Background: I reviewed Alex Morgan in clinic today. The primary carer attended and reported significant fatigue related to round‑the‑clock caregiving responsibilities, including disrupted sleep due to night-time monitoring and coordination of respite arrangements. The caregiving context has been challenging over recent months, and the carer requested documentation to support access to additional respite and workplace flexibility. Seizure History Since Last Review: In December 3 generalised tonic-clonic seizures were reported. In March two nocturnal seizures occurred, and in June another during respite care. These events were described by the primary carer and corroborated by respite staff notes in June. There were no reported injuries, tongue bites, or prolonged post‑ictal confusional states requiring emergency services; however, the carer noted marked tiredness for 24–36 hours after each episode. Current Treatment and Tolerability: The patient is taking Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily as reported by the carer. Adherence is generally good with a weekly pill organiser; one missed evening dose was acknowledged in late May. Side effects reported include intermittent irritability and reduced appetite attributed by the carer to Levetiracetam; no rash or ataxia reported. Vitamin D3 1,000 IU daily continues through primary care. Aetiology and Investigations: No new structural aetiology has been identified. A prior MRI (2017) reportedly showed no focal lesion. Routine blood tests arranged by the GP in April (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D) were within reference limits per shared records. The carer requested repeat safety bloods given ongoing fatigue. Functional and Social Context: The carer describes cumulative sleep deprivation due to nocturnal monitoring and disrupted routines following the March events. They report resilience but are seeking increased respite frequency and assistance with transport to appointments. The patient engages with a day activity group twice weekly when available. Risk and Safety: The carer uses a simple nocturnal alert device and maintains a written seizure log. Post‑ictal supervision is available at home, and rescue medication is not currently prescribed. There is no reported alcohol or recreational drug use. The home environment has been adjusted to reduce fall risk (padded headboard, shower seat). Driving is not undertaken. Management Plan: - Continue current Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam at the present doses pending review of adherence and tolerability. - Arrange serum Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam trough levels, FBC, U&E, LFT, and vitamin D via our phlebotomy clinic. - Provide a letter supporting the carer’s request for enhanced respite provision and flexibility at work, citing night-time disruption and recent seizure pattern. - Offer carer support signposting to local services and a fatigue management leaflet; carer accepts. - Reinforce seizure diary completion, including potential triggers, missed doses, and recovery times. - Discussed, patient- and carer‑reported: if further events occur, we will consider rationalising therapy and exploring alternative options after blood results and adherence review. - Follow‑up in 4 months, sooner if there are further convulsive events or concerns from the carer. Yours sincerely,

rows.note_text: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Emma Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 19 November 2023 10:15 To: epilepsy.centre@nhs.net Cc: Dr Michael Byrne (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Nair (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Deterioration during exam period and medication adjustment Hi Emma Epilepsy Diagnosis: Type not classified at present pending further evaluation Present Medication: 1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily 2. Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily 3. Rescue: Buccal midazolam 10 mg as needed for clusters (not used in the past six months) Present Seizure Frequency: Her parents report a reduction in convulsive events, with only a single tonic-clonic seizure over the past six months. Brief myoclonic jerks persist daily on awakening but are considered tolerable. There have been no prolonged or status episodes since treatment escalation. Context and Current Concerns: Despite the above, her overall condition is deteriorating functionally during the current exam/professional assessment season. She and her parents describe marked escalation in stress, poor sleep continuity, early morning awakenings, and increasing pre-ictal symptoms (auras with sudden disequilibrium and visual fuzziness) on study days. There has been a noticeable increase in near-miss episodes with transient loss of awareness lasting a few seconds, occurring several times per week, especially on mornings following late-night revision. Teachers have raised concern about declining concentration, slowed processing speed, and missed coursework deadlines. Weight has remained stable; no intercurrent illness or head injury reported. Adherence is reported as good. No alcohol or recreational drug use. Investigations/Monitoring to Date: - Last EEG (6 months ago): non-specific diffuse fast activity; no clear lateralising features. - MRI brain (last year): unremarkable. - Recent bloods (last month): FBC, U&E, LFTs within normal limits; lamotrigine level mid-therapeutic. Plan of Action: Given the stress-related deterioration in day-to-day functioning and the increased frequency of brief lapses in awareness during the exam period, I recommend the following adjustments and supports: 1) Brivaracetam optimisation: increase to 100 mg in the morning and 125 mg at night for 1 week, then 125 mg twice daily thereafter if tolerated. Monitor for mood changes and excessive sedation. If troublesome somnolence occurs, revert to 100 mg twice daily and notify the clinic. 2) Lamotrigine: maintain 150 mg twice daily for now. If myoclonic jerks intensify or morning lapses persist after brivaracetam optimisation, we will consider a cautious increase to 175 mg twice daily at the next review. 3) Rescue strategy: retain buccal midazolam 10 mg for clusters or prolonged events; parents and school have updated care plan and know administration protocol. 4) Lifestyle and stress mitigation: strict sleep schedule with 7–8 hours nightly, avoid late-night revision sessions, schedule breaks during study, regular hydration and balanced meals. She has been referred to our neuropsychology-led stress management group and to the hospital education liaison team for exam accommodations (quiet room, rest breaks, extra time as needed). 5) Safety: reinforce seizure first aid with school/assessment centre. Avoid unsupervised swimming and heights. Consider temporary pause on driving applications until spells of altered awareness have resolved and we have clarified nature of events. 6) Further evaluation: book an ambulatory EEG during a representative study week to capture brief lapses; if non-diagnostic, proceed to short-term video-EEG telemetry. We will also obtain an updated cognitive screening profile to quantify the impact of stress on attention and processing speed. Follow-up has been arranged in 8 weeks, sooner if events escalate or any tonic-clonic seizures recur. Please advise us promptly if there are mood changes on the higher brivaracetam dose or if the brief lapses become longer or more frequent. With best wishes

This 23-year-old student lives on a moored houseboat and reports occasional power outages that sometimes delay charging of her phone and medication reminder device. She keeps medications in a dry, insulated container and has not missed doses in the past two months by her account. Her parents accompany her to clinic and corroborate the recent history. rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Kate Health Centre Keele University, Keele, Newcastle Staffordshire ST5 5BG Dear Dr Kate Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: K594203 NHS No. 7719826405 12 Larch Close, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 1AB Diagnoses/summary: Idiopathic generalised epilepsy with previous generalised tonic–clonic and myoclonic seizures; patient has generalised epilepsy. EEG (2023): Generalised spike–wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy phenotype. Previous medication: valproate (effective but weight gain), levetiracetam (behavioural adverse effects), topiramate (cognitive slowing), lamotrigine (partial benefit), clonazepam PRN; trial of zonisamide discontinued due to renal colic. Since VNS parameter optimisation at his previous appointment, he feels substantially better in day-to-day functioning and reports improved confidence with community activities. Family and employer feedback has been positive. Sleep routine has become more regular and he has resumed light exercise. He denies new adverse effects aside from occasional throat paraesthesia at stimulation onset, which he finds tolerable. Appetite and weight have stabilised. Mood is described as “more even”, with no self-harm thoughts. He has continued to use the VNS magnet for auras, reporting that it often shortens events. Seizure control: His family corroborate a clear decline in convulsive activity; there has been only one generalised tonic–clonic event over roughly half a year. Brief myoclonic twitches still occur on some mornings, typically once a month on waking, but these are short and manageable. Importantly, there have been no prolonged seizures, clusters requiring attendance, or status episodes since the VNS changes. Weight stable at 74 kg. BP 122/74, pulse 68 regular. â€ Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. - Maintain current VNS settings given clinical response; no change required today. Provided education on magnet use and avoidance of common seizure triggers (sleep deprivation, missed doses, excess alcohol). Ã© - Bloods today: U&E, LFT, FBC to monitor ongoing therapy; thyroid function given patient enquiry about fatigue previously. - Seizure diary to continue; encouraged ongoing lifestyle regularity and hydration. - DVLA guidance reiterated; he confirms adherence and understands the requirements. - Routine follow-up in 6 months, earlier if breakthrough convulsions or adverse effects; remote nurse call in 8 weeks to check stability. Overall, there has been a sustained and meaningful improvement in control since VNS optimisation, with better quality of life and no prolonged events. Thank you for your ongoing support in primary care, including prescription continuation and monitoring of bloods. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Wang Saffron Park Hospital Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL Dear Dr Wang John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746 Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL Thank you for asking me to review your patient in the Neurology Clinic today. Since my last assessment in March 2025, her diary and a menstrual tracking app together suggest a catamenial pattern to her events, with clusters tending to occur from two days before menstruation through day three of her cycle. She has been diligent in logging symptoms, sleep times, and medication doses. Current medication at the time of review is: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily, Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, and Clobazam 5 mg at night; she also uses Folic Acid 400 micrograms once daily. She previously trialled Zonisamide (discontinued in January 2025 due to appetite loss and low mood) and a brief course of Brivaracetam (stopped due to dizziness without clear benefit). She reports mild fatigue in the late afternoon but no rash, diplopia, or significant mood lability. Liver function and full blood count from July 2025 were within reference limits. Her parents accompany her today and corroborate the pattern described. Her parents report a reduction in convulsive events, with only a single tonic-clonic seizure over the past six months. Brief myoclonic jerks persist monthly on awakening but are considered tolerable. There have been no prolonged or status episodes since treatment escalation. She notes that sleep disruption the night before menses remains a consistent trigger, and she has been using phone reminders around the perimenstrual window to reinforce adherence. There have been no injuries or emergency department attendances. We discussed that, while the temporal association with her cycle is suggestive, we have not altered treatment pending further corroboration. She is agreeable to continuing her seizure and menstrual logging for another two cycles, and she has consented to share the app export with our service. She has also requested information about non-hormonal strategies for perimenstrual symptom management; I have provided written resources and signposted the epilepsy specialist nurse for practical support. She is not planning pregnancy in the next year and understands the need to contact us early if this changes. I will arrange a routine EEG with sleep deprivation and update you with the findings. For now, I have advised no medication changes and to maintain current dosing times. I will review her again in three months, sooner if there is any deterioration or recurrence of convulsive activity. Yours sincerely

rows.note_text: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Fiona Centre for Epilepsy Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Fiona, Thomas Reed, DOB: 22-11-1991, Hospital No: R528410 NHS No. 8742153690 Flat 3, 45 Bloomsbury Way, London, WC1A 2SE Epilepsy – Focal Epilepsy Type Medication: Previously on Levetiracetam up to 1,500 mg twice daily (stopped due to mood irritability); prior trial of Carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily (discontinued for hyponatraemia). Lacosamide Blood Level: 18th September 2025: 6.1 µg/mL (reference 1–10 µg/mL). Dose 150 mg twice daily. Seizures: He has experienced ongoing focal impaired-awareness seizures, typically four episodes monthly. These are occasionally accompanied by brief disorientation but resolve spontaneously. No generalised tonic-clonic seizures have occurred since last year. Caregivers feel overall control is acceptable. I reviewed Thomas Reed today in face-to-face clinic following reports of increased difficulties on workdays. He has a confirmed diagnosis of focal epilepsy arising from the left temporal region on prior EEG and semiology. Over the past three months he describes a deterioration in day-to-day functioning, with more frequent clustering of focal events Monday–Thursday, coinciding with periods of high workload and extended screen time. He notes brief post-event fatigue and word-finding pauses (Ã‚Â·), though he recovers without assistance. Sleep is fragmented during deadlines and missed meals are common. There have been no injuries, tongue bites, or incontinence. No recent intercurrent illness, alcohol excess, or missed doses reported; however, he admits to taking evening Zonisamide later than planned on late shifts (ï¿½). Examination today was non-focal neurologically; BP 128/76, pulse 68 regular. Weight stable at 74 kg. Mood mildly anxious by report; no suicidal ideation. Adverse effects: intermittent paraesthesiae in fingers thought possibly Zonisamide-related; no diplopia, ataxia, or notable dizziness. Work and safety: Events tend to cluster on workdays per patient report, with two episodes occurring at his desk in the last month, each lasting ~60–90 seconds and characterised by behavioural arrest, staring, and subsequent brief disorientation (â€). He has informed his line manager and is currently avoiding lone high-risk tasks; he does not drive and remains compliant with DVLA guidance. Investigations: Latest routine bloods (U&E, LFTs, bicarbonate) on 18/09/2025 normal; bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. Repeat EEG and MRI (3T epilepsy protocol) were previously performed in 2023 showing left mesial temporal sclerosis; no interval imaging since. Discussion today: Although caregivers perceive overall control as acceptable, both patient and clinician note a deterioration in functional impact with weekday clustering and greater post-ictal fatigue. Given the temporal association with workload and suboptimal sleep, we discussed structured sleep hygiene, scheduled meal breaks, and stress-modulation strategies. He will continue a seizure diary with specific annotation of work-related triggers and timing (Ã©). We also discussed the option of optimisation of current anti-seizure medication in due course and will obtain a Zonisamide level to guide any future adjustments. Plan: - Continue Lacosamide 150 mg twice daily and Zonisamide 200 mg nocte for now. - Check Zonisamide trough level and repeat U&E/bicarbonate in 6 weeks. - Arrange ambulatory EEG to capture weekday clustering. - Occupational health referral to consider temporary workload adjustments and regular protected breaks. - Provide written seizure first-aid guidance to employer; patient to avoid lone work at heights or near open water/unguarded machinery (ï¿½). - Telephone review in 8 weeks; earlier if seizure frequency increases or any generalised events occur. I will update you following results. Please let me know if any concerns are raised by his workplace or caregivers in the interim. Yours sincerely
